This guide covers what exclusive concrete leads should actually cost, the contract clauses that should make you walk, and why performance-based pricing is the only structure that aligns an agency's incentives with your crew's schedule.

What exclusive concrete leads actually cost in 2026

Benchmark pricing before any agency conversation, because the first number you hear will anchor the deal. For exclusive, real-time leads generated through Meta or Google Ads, here's the realistic range by job type:

  • Driveways and patios: $60–$120 per exclusive lead. Average job value $6,000–$15,000.
  • Stamped and decorative concrete: $80–$150. Higher intent, higher ticket, longer sales cycle.
  • Foundations and slabs: $100–$200. Fewer searches, but a single closed job can be $20,000+.
  • Commercial flatwork: $150–$300. Low volume, long cycles, massive contract values.

Compare that to shared marketplace leads at $40–$80 that convert at 10–15% because four competitors got the same phone number. An exclusive $100 lead closing at 25–30% produces a cost-per-acquisition of $330–$400. A shared $60 lead closing at 12% costs you $500 per job — plus the hours your estimator burned chasing dead numbers.

The metric that matters is never cost per lead. It's cost per booked estimate and cost per signed contract. Any agency that can't speak in those terms in the first call is selling you traffic, not revenue.

Shared leads are a tax on contractors who don't run their own ads

The marketplace model — Angi, Thumbtack, HomeAdvisor — is built on selling the same homeowner to multiple contractors and letting you fight over them. That structure guarantees three problems.

First, speed becomes everything. Studies of inbound lead response consistently show contact rates collapse after the first five minutes, and with shared leads you're racing four other estimators to the same phone. Second, price becomes the only lever. When a homeowner has five bids in hand, the conversation starts at 'what's your number' instead of 'what's your process.' Third, you build zero assets. Every dollar spent on marketplace leads rents attention the platform owns.

A real lead generation agency inverts this. They run ads under your brand, drive homeowners to your landing page, and every lead knows your company name before they pick up the phone. The pixel data, the ad account history, the retargeting audiences — those compound for you, not for a marketplace. Six months of exclusive campaign data is an asset you keep even if you fire the agency. Six months of Thumbtack spend is a receipt.

Red flags in agency contracts that should end the conversation

Concrete is a vertical where mediocre agencies hide easily, because seasonality masks bad performance. Watch for these clauses before signing:

  • They own the ad account. If campaigns run inside the agency's Meta Business Manager or Google Ads account, you lose all history, audiences, and learning data the day you leave. Non-negotiable: the account lives in YOUR Business Manager, with the agency added as a partner.
  • 12-month lock-ins with no performance out. A confident agency offers 90-day terms or a performance clause. A 12-month term with no exit tied to lead volume means they're monetizing the contract, not the campaigns.
  • No lead definition in writing. What counts as a lead? A form fill? A connected call over 60 seconds? A qualified homeowner in your service area? If it's not defined, you'll pay for wrong numbers and out-of-area inquiries.
  • Vague reporting. If the monthly report shows impressions and clicks but not cost per booked estimate, they're reporting activity, not outcomes. Demand call tracking and a shared dashboard — Google Analytics plus a CRM like GoHighLevel makes this trivial to provide.
  • 'Proprietary lead sources' they won't name. That usually means they're reselling aged data or arbitraging the same marketplaces you're trying to escape.

Why performance-based deals beat retainers in this vertical

Concrete work is seasonal, ticket sizes are large, and demand is geographically lumpy. That combination makes flat retainers structurally wrong for most contractors.

On a $3,500/month retainer, the agency gets paid the same whether they deliver 60 leads in June or 11 in January. Every incentive points toward doing just enough to keep the invoice going. In a performance deal — per exclusive lead, per booked estimate, or a hybrid base-plus-performance — the agency only eats when you do.

Three structures work in this trade:

  1. Pure pay-per-lead: $80–$150 per exclusive, qualified lead with a written lead definition and a replacement policy for junk. Simplest to audit.
  2. Pay-per-booked-estimate: $150–$300 per appointment that shows on your calendar. Costs more per unit but shifts qualification work onto the agency.
  3. Hybrid: Small management fee ($1,000–$1,500) covering ad ops, plus per-lead pricing. Fair when the agency is also building landing pages and follow-up automation.

One caveat: pure performance deals only attract good agencies when your close rate is credible. If you take three days to call leads back, no competent performance partner will touch the account — they'd be subsidizing your slow follow-up. Fix speed-to-lead first, then negotiate on performance.

The follow-up system matters more than the ad budget

Here's what most contractors miss: lead generation fails at the phone, not the ad. An agency can deliver 50 qualified leads a month, and a contractor who calls back 'when the crew breaks for lunch' will close almost none of them.

The contractors winning this game run automated follow-up the moment a lead lands:

  • Instant SMS + email within 60 seconds of form submission, from a system like GoHighLevel — 'Thanks for reaching out about your driveway, when's a good time for a quick call?'
  • AI voice or missed-call text-back so an after-hours lead at 8 p.m. gets a response at 8:01, not 9 a.m. tomorrow.
  • A 12-touch nurture sequence over 30 days, because a homeowner planning a $12,000 patio might take three weeks to decide — and the contractor still texting on day 20 is usually the one who signs.
  • Calendar booking links (Calendly or built into your CRM) so estimates get scheduled without phone tag.

When you evaluate agencies, ask what happens in the 10 minutes after a lead submits. The good ones have a documented answer with automation behind it. The mediocre ones say 'we send you the lead and you take it from there.' That handoff gap is where 40% of your ad spend quietly dies.

Questions that separate real operators from resellers

Use these in the sales call. The answers tell you everything:

  1. 'Show me a live campaign for another concrete or flatwork client.' Not a case study PDF — a screen share of Meta Ads Manager or Google Ads. Real operators can show anonymized dashboards. Resellers stall.
  2. 'What's your average cost per booked estimate in this vertical?' They should quote a range and explain what moves it — service area density, job type, season. A blank stare means they've never tracked it.
  3. 'Who owns the ad account, the landing pages, and the phone numbers?' The only acceptable answer is you. Tracking numbers especially — if the agency owns the number your Google Business Profile has accumulated, they own your call volume when you leave.
  4. 'What's your lead replacement policy?' Wrong numbers, out-of-area, spam — a written policy replacing those within 48 hours is standard among agencies that trust their own targeting.
  5. 'How many concrete clients do you have in my market?' More than one in your service area means they're bidding against you with your own money. Demand market exclusivity in writing.

Any agency that handles all five without flinching is worth a 90-day test. Anyone who dodges two or more is a middleman with a Canva deck.

How to structure a 90-day test that produces a real verdict

Don't sign annual deals on faith. Run a structured 90-day pilot with defined success criteria and enough budget to generate statistically meaningful data.

Days 1–14: Foundation. Agency builds landing pages, installs tracking (call tracking, form tracking, GA4 events), sets up your CRM pipeline, and launches campaigns in YOUR ad account. If setup takes more than two weeks, that's your first data point.

Days 15–45: Calibration. Expect cost per lead to run 20–30% above benchmark while the algorithm learns and creative gets tested. Judge the agency on iteration speed — are they testing new hooks, adjusting geo-targeting, killing losing ads weekly? Meta's learning phase rewards decisive operators.

Days 46–90: Verdict window. Now the numbers count. Minimum viable performance for a residential concrete contractor spending $2,500–$4,000/month on ads: 25–40 exclusive leads monthly, 40%+ lead-to-estimate rate, and at least 3–5 signed jobs directly attributed to the campaign. At a $9,000 average ticket, that's $27,000–$45,000 in contracted revenue against roughly $10,000–$14,000 in total spend.

Put those thresholds in the agreement. If the agency hits them, scale budget 25–50% in month four. If they miss and can't show a credible fix, you walk with your ad account, your data, and your landing pages intact — because you structured ownership correctly on day one.

The bottom line

Hiring a lead generation agency as a concrete contractor comes down to three decisions made before any contract is signed: exclusive leads only, performance-aligned pricing, and full ownership of every asset the campaigns create. Get those three right and even a mediocre agency can't hurt you badly. Get them wrong and even a talented one will cost you a season.

The contractors dominating their markets right now aren't the ones with the biggest ad budgets — they're the ones who pair exclusive lead flow with 60-second follow-up and hold their agency to cost-per-signed-job, not clicks. Run the 90-day test, measure what matters, and scale what proves itself.

faq.question: How much should concrete contractors pay per exclusive lead?
faq.answer: For residential work like driveways and patios, expect $60–$120 per exclusive lead from Meta or Google Ads. Decorative and stamped concrete runs $80–$150, foundations $100–$200, and commercial flatwork $150–$300. The better metric is cost per signed job — with a 25–30% close rate on exclusive leads, a healthy account lands between $330 and $500 per contracted project.

faq.question: Are shared leads from Angi or Thumbtack worth it for concrete contractors?
faq.answer: Rarely. Shared leads get sold to three to five contractors simultaneously, dropping close rates to 10–15% and forcing price-first conversations. A $60 shared lead closing at 12% costs about $500 per job — more than a $100 exclusive lead closing at 25% — and you build no brand or ad-data assets in the process.

faq.question: Should I choose a retainer or performance-based lead generation deal?
faq.answer: Performance-based or hybrid pricing fits concrete better than flat retainers because demand is seasonal and job values are high. Pay-per-lead ($80–$150), pay-per-booked-estimate ($150–$300), or a small management fee plus per-lead pricing all keep the agency's incentives tied to your pipeline. Flat retainers pay agencies the same in January as in June — you carry all the seasonal risk.

faq.question: What should be in the contract before I hire a lead generation agency?
faq.answer: Five things in writing: you own the ad accounts, landing pages, and tracking phone numbers; a specific lead definition (qualified homeowner, in service area, valid contact info); a junk-lead replacement policy within 48 hours; market exclusivity in your service area; and 90-day terms or a performance exit clause instead of a 12-month lock-in.

faq.question: How long does it take for concrete lead generation campaigns to work?
faq.answer: Expect two weeks of setup, then a 30-day calibration window where costs run 20–30% above benchmark while creative and targeting are tested. Judge results in days 46–90: a $2,500–$4,000 monthly ad budget should produce 25–40 exclusive leads per month, a 40%+ estimate rate, and 3–5 signed jobs. If those thresholds aren't met by day 90, walk.

articles.title: Hire a Lead Generation Agency for Concrete Contractors: Real Costs
articles.description: What concrete contractors should pay per exclusive lead, contract red flags to avoid, and why performance deals crush retainers. Straight from the media buy desk.
articles.keyword: hire lead generation agency for concrete contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most concrete contractors are getting hosed by lead gen agencies. The going rate for an "exclusive" concrete lead in 2025 sits between $65 and $180 depending on market and job type — driveways at the low end, decorative and commercial pours at the high end. If you're paying a $3,500/month retainer and getting 12 shared leads that also went to three other guys, you're not buying leads. You're buying someone's Meta Ads experiment. This article is for concrete contractors, hardscape crews, and decorative concrete shops doing $500K to $10M in revenue who are tired of tire-kickers, price shoppers, and "leads" that never answer the phone. It's also for owners who've been burned by an agency once and want to know how to vet the next one. Here's what you'll get: benchmark cost-per-lead by job type, the exact contract clauses that signal you're about to be locked into garbage, and why pay-per-lead or pay-per-appointment beats retainers in this vertical every single time.

What an exclusive concrete lead actually costs in 2025

Let's kill the fantasy pricing first. If an agency is telling you they can deliver exclusive concrete leads for $25 a pop, they're either lying, running bait ads that attract broke homeowners, or planning to resell that lead to two other contractors and call it "exclusive to your zip code." Here are the real numbers I see across Meta Ads Manager and Google Ads accounts for concrete contractors: - Residential driveway leads (exclusive): $65–$95

  • Patio and flatwork leads: $75–$120
  • Decorative/stamped concrete: $110–$180
  • Commercial pours and foundations: $150–$400
  • Booked appointments (qualified, on calendar): $200–$450 These assume the agency is running paid traffic on Meta or Google, using a landing page with instant lead routing (typically through GoHighLevel or a HubSpot workflow), and calling or texting the lead within 5 minutes. If any of those pieces are missing, your cost-per-closed-job doubles. A healthy close rate on properly qualified concrete leads is 20-30%. That puts your customer acquisition cost between $250 and $900. If your average job is $6,500 and your gross margin is 35%, you can pay up to $2,200 per acquired customer before the math stops working. Know these numbers before you sign anything.

Why retainers are structurally rigged against contractors

The standard agency retainer — $2,500 to $5,000/month plus ad spend — transfers all the risk to you. The agency gets paid whether their campaigns produce or not. They have zero financial incentive to hit a specific cost-per-lead because their revenue is fixed. Watch what happens on month three. The novelty wears off, your account gets handed to a junior media buyer, and the "strategist" you signed with is now onboarding new clients. Your ad account slowly drifts. Frequency creeps up, creative gets stale, CPLs climb 40%, and when you complain, you get a slide deck about "seasonality." The incentive structure matters more than the pitch. Under a retainer, the agency's job is to keep you subscribed. Under a pay-per-lead or pay-per-appointment deal, the agency's job is to make the phone ring. Those are completely different daily behaviors. The only time a retainer makes sense for a concrete contractor: 1. You're doing $5M+ and need a dedicated team managing SEO, paid, CRM, and reputation as one system 2. You already have an in-house sales manager who can hold the agency accountable weekly 3. The retainer includes hard performance guarantees with credits for missed targets Otherwise, retainers are a subsidy from you to the agency's overhead.

The performance-based deal structures that actually work

There are three deal structures that align incentives correctly for concrete work: 1. Pure pay-per-lead (PPL): You pay a flat fee per qualified lead delivered — usually $75–$150. Agency covers ad spend. Best for contractors who already have a fast, disciplined sales process. Risk: agencies may relax lead qualification to hit volume. 2. Pay-per-appointment (PPA): You pay $250–$450 per confirmed appointment on your calendar (via Calendly or GoHighLevel booking). Agency handles ads, qualification, and setting. This is my preferred structure for most $1M–$5M concrete shops. You literally only pay when someone shows up on your calendar with a real project. 3. Revenue share on booked jobs: Agency takes 8-15% of gross revenue from closed jobs they sourced. Requires tight attribution and trust on both sides. Works best when you already have a working relationship. Rare, but the highest-alignment structure that exists. Whatever structure you pick, define "qualified" in writing. For concrete, a qualified lead means: homeowner or decision-maker, property in your service area, project starting within 90 days, budget floor of $3,000, and answered the phone or replied within 24 hours. Anything less than that spec and you shouldn't be paying for it.

Seven red flags to look for in the agency contract

Contracts tell you what an agency actually plans to do — not what the sales guy promised on the Zoom call. Read every line before signing. 1. 12-month minimums with no performance out clause. Standard predatory move. Insist on a 90-day performance window with defined KPIs, and a 30-day out if targets are missed two months running. 2. Ad account ownership held by the agency. If they run ads through their Business Manager and you leave, you lose all pixel data, audience history, and campaign learning. Non-negotiable: the ad account must be in your Meta Business Manager, with them added as a partner. 3. No cost-per-lead guarantee or benchmark. If they won't put a target CPL in writing, they don't know their numbers or they don't want you to know theirs. 4. "Lead" defined as any form fill. A form fill from a bot or a 19-year-old renter isn't a lead. Define qualification criteria in the SOW. 5. Shared leads dressed up as exclusive. Ask directly: "Is this lead sold to any other contractor, ever?" Get it in writing. 6. Automatic renewal clauses buried on page 8. Auto-renewal is fine if you have to opt out 30 days prior. If it's 90 days, they're playing games. 7. No reporting access. You should have direct login access to Google Analytics, Meta Ads Manager, and the CRM. If reporting is a weekly PDF only, you're being managed, not served.

How to vet a lead gen agency in 30 minutes

You don't need three sales calls to figure out if an agency is legit. You need the right questions and the discipline to walk away when the answers are weak. Ask these on the first call: - "Show me a live ad account for a current concrete client." Not a case study PDF. A screen share of Meta Ads Manager showing spend, CPL, and conversion volume for the last 90 days. If they can't or won't, next.

  • "What's your average CPL for driveway leads in a market like mine?" If they can't answer within $20, they haven't run enough concrete campaigns.
  • "Who specifically will run my account, and how many other accounts do they manage?" Anything over 12 accounts per media buyer means your account gets scraps.
  • "What happens in month 4 when creative fatigues?" Correct answer: we produce 4-8 new creatives per month using UGC-style video from your job sites. Wrong answer: vague talk about "optimization."
  • "Can I talk to two current clients — not references you've prepped?" Any agency worth hiring can produce this within 48 hours. Also check: do they use GoHighLevel or a comparable CRM for lead routing and speed-to-lead automation? If lead handoff is manual — email forwarding to your inbox — your close rate will crater. Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes doubles contact rates in home services. That's not optional infrastructure.

What you need to have in place before hiring anyone

The best lead gen agency in the country can't fix a broken sales process. Before you write a check, get these five things locked down or you'll waste every lead they send. 1. A dedicated phone line and someone to answer it. Not a cell that gets checked between pours. Missed calls from paid leads are $150 setting on fire. Use a tracking number (CallRail or the number inside GoHighLevel) so you can measure answer rate. 2. Speed-to-lead automation. The moment a lead submits a form, an SMS should fire from your business number, a call task should hit your setter, and a follow-up email should queue. GoHighLevel handles this out of the box; so does HubSpot with a paid seat. 3. A defined qualification script. 6-8 questions max: project type, square footage, timeline, budget, decision-maker, property address, how they heard about you. Ninety seconds on the phone. 4. A CRM with pipeline stages. New Lead → Contacted → Estimate Scheduled → Estimate Delivered → Won/Lost. Without stage tracking, you can't measure close rate and the agency will get blamed for your sales problem. 5. A follow-up cadence for the 70% who don't buy immediately. Seven touches over 30 days via SMS and email. Most concrete jobs close 15-45 days after first contact. If you drop them after two calls, you're leaving 40% of the pipeline unclosed.

The math: when hiring an agency actually makes sense

Not every concrete contractor should hire a lead gen agency. Run this math before you engage anyone. Take your average job value × your gross margin percentage. That's your max acquisition cost per customer. For a shop averaging $8,000 jobs at 32% gross margin, that's $2,560 you can spend to acquire a customer and still make money. Now assume you close 25% of qualified leads. You can spend up to $640 per qualified lead ($2,560 × 0.25) before losing money on average — though you want to spend far less to actually profit. If an agency delivers exclusive leads at $120 and you close 25%, your CAC is $480. That's profitable. Here's when it doesn't work: - Average job under $2,000 with thin margins. The math doesn't support paid lead acquisition. Focus on referrals, Google Business Profile optimization, and Nextdoor.

  • Close rate under 15%. Fix sales first. No agency will save you.
  • You can't handle 15+ new estimates a month. Overwhelmed contractors deliver bad estimates, lose bids, and blame the agency. When the math works — average ticket $5K+, close rate 20%+, capacity to handle volume — a performance-based agency deal is one of the highest-ROI moves you can make. When it doesn't, no amount of Meta spend will fix it.

The bottom line

Hiring a lead generation agency for concrete work is straightforward once you strip the mystery out of it. Know the real cost of a lead in your market. Refuse retainers unless there's a specific reason to justify one. Insist on pay-per-lead or pay-per-appointment structures with written qualification criteria. Read the contract. Own your ad account. Vet the media buyer, not the salesperson. The contractors who scale profitably with paid lead gen aren't the ones who found a magic agency. They're the ones who built a fast, disciplined sales process, negotiated aligned incentives, and held their agency accountable to weekly numbers. Do those three things and the leads take care of themselves.

faq.question: How much should I pay for an exclusive concrete lead?
faq.answer: For residential driveways and flatwork, $65–$120 per exclusive lead is fair. Decorative and stamped concrete runs $110–$180. Commercial work is $150–$400. If someone quotes below $50 for exclusive, verify it's not being resold to other contractors.

faq.question: Is pay-per-lead or a monthly retainer better for concrete contractors?
faq.answer: Pay-per-lead or pay-per-appointment is almost always better for contractors under $5M in revenue. It aligns the agency's incentive with your outcomes and eliminates the risk of paying $3K/month for underperforming campaigns. Retainers only make sense when you have in-house oversight and multi-channel scope.

faq.question: How long before I see results from a lead gen agency?
faq.answer: Meta and Google campaigns for concrete typically produce qualified leads within 7-14 days of launch. Real optimization — where CPLs stabilize and creative wins are identified — takes 45-60 days. Any agency promising results in week one is either lucky or overpromising.

faq.question: Should the agency own my Facebook ad account?
faq.answer: No. The ad account must live in your Meta Business Manager with the agency added as a partner. If they own it, you lose the pixel history, custom audiences, and campaign learning the moment you leave. This is non-negotiable.

faq.question: What's a realistic close rate on paid concrete leads?
faq.answer: 20-30% on properly qualified exclusive leads, assuming you answer the phone within 5 minutes and follow up consistently for 30 days. Shared leads or slow follow-up drops that to 5-10%. Your close rate is the single biggest lever in whether paid lead gen is profitable.

articles.title: How to Structure Google Ads for Multi-Location Service Businesses
articles.description: A media buyer's blueprint for structuring Google Ads across multiple locations: geo-segmented campaigns, SKAGs vs Performance Max, and a budget decision tree.
articles.keyword: lead generation for commercial solar installers
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most multi-location service businesses run Google Ads with one campaign, one geo radius drawn around everything, and one shared budget. Then they wonder why their strongest market prints leads while three other locations starve. The auction doesn't care about fairness — it routes spend to wherever clicks are cheapest, which is almost never where your growth capacity is.

Campaign structure is the single highest-leverage decision in a multi-location account. Not the ads, not the keywords, not even the landing pages. Structure determines how budget flows, what Smart Bidding learns, and whether you can even see which location is profitable. Get it wrong and every optimization downstream is built on noise.

This is the architecture we deploy for multi-location service clients — when to segment by location, when geo-targeted single keyword ad groups earn their overhead, where Performance Max actually belongs, and a decision tree based on the two variables that matter: location count and monthly budget.

Why one shared campaign quietly starves your growth markets

When five locations share one campaign, Google allocates budget by auction efficiency, not business priority. Your Dallas location has been open six years, has 400 reviews, and converts at 12%. Your new San Antonio location has 30 reviews and converts at 6%. Smart Bidding will shovel 70% of spend into Dallas because that's where conversions are cheapest — even if Dallas is already at capacity and San Antonio is the location you opened the campaign to grow.

Shared campaigns also destroy your reporting. Location-level performance gets buried in geo reports most operators never open, so the P&L conversation becomes 'Google Ads costs $8K and drives 90 leads' instead of 'San Antonio's CPL is $140 versus Dallas at $52, and here's why.' You cannot manage what you've blended.

The third failure is bid strategy contamination. Target CPA works by learning conversion patterns. A mature market and a launch market have fundamentally different patterns — mixing them in one campaign forces the algorithm to optimize toward an average that describes neither. The fix isn't smarter bidding. It's separation: each location (or market cluster) gets its own campaign, its own budget line, and its own conversion history. That's the foundation everything else sits on.

The core architecture: one campaign per market, not per service

The default instinct is to structure by service line — a 'Water Heater' campaign, a 'Drain Cleaning' campaign — with all locations lumped inside. Invert it. For multi-location service businesses, geography is the primary segmentation axis and service is secondary.

The blueprint: one Search campaign per location (or per metro cluster if locations overlap), geo-targeted to that location's realistic service radius using 'presence' targeting — not 'presence or interest,' which leaks spend to people researching from out of market. Inside each campaign, ad groups segment by service line. So it's 'Search – San Antonio' containing ad groups for water heaters, drains, and repipes — not the reverse.

Why this direction? Three reasons. Budget control lives at the campaign level, and budget decisions in multi-location businesses are location decisions. Second, Smart Bidding learns per campaign, and market-level conversion behavior (competition, pricing tolerance, brand strength) varies more by geography than by service. Third, your reporting now mirrors your org chart — each location manager sees their own campaign, their own CPL, their own call volume.

Set radius targeting from actual job data, not guesses. Pull 12 months of completed jobs from your CRM or GoHighLevel, map the ZIP codes covering 85% of revenue, and target those. Most businesses over-draw their radius by 40% and pay for clicks they'd never profitably serve.

Geo-targeted SKAGs: when granularity actually pays

Single keyword ad groups got a bad reputation because people deployed them everywhere, then drowned in management overhead when close variants blurred match types. But in a geo-segmented account, a modified version still outperforms — for a specific slice of your keywords.

The play: take your highest-intent, highest-ticket keywords — 'water heater replacement,' 'emergency plumber,' 'ac installation' — and give each its own ad group per location campaign, with responsive search ads written to mirror the exact query plus the city name. 'Water Heater Replacement in San Antonio — Licensed, Same-Day' against the query 'water heater replacement san antonio' produces the message match that drives quality scores of 8–10, and every point of quality score cuts your effective CPC roughly 10–15%.

Don't SKAG everything. Long-tail and research queries go into consolidated thematic ad groups where Smart Bidding has enough volume to learn. The threshold I use: if a keyword drives 15+ clicks a month in that market and the average job value clears $500, it earns its own ad group. Below that, consolidate.

This hybrid — SKAGs for the head terms, themed groups for the tail — gets you the relevance premium where it's worth money and the algorithmic efficiency where it isn't. Pure SKAG accounts and pure broad-consolidation accounts both leave margin on the table; the operators winning multi-location auctions run the blend.

Where Performance Max belongs (and where it will hurt you)

Performance Max is not a replacement for Search in a service business. It's a supplementary layer — and only after your Search foundation is feeding it clean conversion data.

The sequencing matters. PMax optimizes toward whatever conversions you feed it. Launch it on day one with no conversion history and it will find the cheapest possible 'conversions' — often low-quality form fills, accidental calls under 30 seconds, and remarketing clicks from people who would have converted anyway. Launch it after 90 days of Search generating verified lead conversions (qualified calls over 60 seconds, booked appointments synced from your CRM), and it has a real target.

Where PMax earns its keep for multi-location businesses: capturing demand Search can't see — Maps placements, YouTube, Discover, Gmail — and defending your local brand terms across surfaces. One PMax campaign per major market, fed with location-specific asset groups, typically adds 15–25% incremental lead volume at a CPL 20–30% above Search. That's acceptable as expansion. It's a disaster as a foundation.

Two non-negotiables: enable per-location asset groups with real photos of that location's team and trucks (stock imagery tanks engagement in local service), and review your search terms insights weekly. PMax will drift toward brand and near-brand queries to flatter its own numbers — carve brand into a separate exact-match Search campaign so you can see true non-brand performance.

The decision tree: match structure to locations and budget

Two variables drive the right structure: how many locations, and how much monthly budget. Here's the tree we run new accounts through.

2–4 locations, under $5K/month: One Search campaign per location, service-based ad groups inside, shared negative keyword list. No PMax yet — the budget can't feed two campaign types enough conversion volume to learn. Every location needs roughly 30 conversions a month for Target CPA to stabilize; below that, use Max Clicks with a CPC ceiling and manage manually.

2–4 locations, $5K–$15K/month: Same Search skeleton, plus SKAG treatment on head terms in your top two markets, plus one PMax campaign covering all locations once Search hits 90 days of clean conversions.

5–10 locations, $15K–$40K/month: Cluster locations into metro-level campaigns where service areas overlap (two locations in one metro share a campaign with radius-split ad groups). Dedicated brand campaign. PMax per major metro. Budget reallocation reviewed weekly against per-location CPL targets.

10+ locations or $40K+/month: This is portfolio management. Campaigns grouped into shared budgets by market tier (mature, growth, launch), portfolio bid strategies per tier, and a formal monthly budget re-ranking based on marginal CPL — move dollars from markets where the next lead costs $180 to markets where it costs $70. At this scale, structure reviews quarterly; markets change tiers.

Landing pages and ad copy: congruence is the multiplier

A perfectly structured account pointing at one generic homepage wastes most of its own advantage. The geo-segmented campaign only pays off when the click lands on a location-specific page that confirms three things in the first screen: you serve this city, you handle this service, and real people nearby chose you.

Minimum viable location page: city name in the H1 and title tag, the specific service front and center, that location's phone number (a tracking number — more on that below), that location's reviews, and photos of that location's actual crew. Businesses that move from one shared landing page to per-location pages routinely see conversion rates improve 30–60% with zero change in traffic. It's the cheapest lift in the entire account.

Ad copy follows the same congruence rule. Every responsive search ad in the San Antonio campaign should pin the city name in at least one headline position. Use location insertion for scale, but write two or three hand-built city headlines per market too — dynamically inserted text reads generic, and in service categories where trust is the buying criterion, 'San Antonio's Highest-Rated Drain Team' beats '{Location} Drain Services' every time.

Extensions are location-level work as well: location assets synced from each Google Business Profile, call assets with per-location tracking numbers, and sitelinks pointing to that market's service pages — never the corporate About page.

Measurement: per-location CPL or you're flying blind

Structure gives you the ability to see per-location performance. Measurement discipline is what makes that visibility real.

First layer: call tracking with per-location numbers. CallRail or WhatConvert, dynamic number insertion on each location page, and a qualification threshold — calls over 60 seconds from new callers count as leads; everything else is noise. Import these as conversions so Smart Bidding optimizes toward qualified calls, not all calls. Accounts optimizing on raw calls typically discover 30–40% of their 'leads' are spam, vendors, and existing customers.

Second layer: close the loop to revenue. Push leads into your CRM tagged by campaign (which now equals location, because your structure made that true), and mark jobs won with job value. Within 90 days you'll have the number that actually matters: cost per booked job by location. That's when budget meetings change — you stop arguing about CPCs and start moving dollars toward the market with the best marginal return.

Third layer: offline conversion import back into Google Ads. Feed booked-job data into the platform and switch mature campaigns to Target ROAS or value-based Target CPA. This is the compounding advantage — while competitors optimize toward clicks and form fills, your bidding learns from revenue. In our experience, accounts running offline conversion import for six months beat call-optimized accounts on cost per booked job by 25–40%, with identical budgets.

The bottom line

Multi-location Google Ads is a structure problem before it's an optimization problem. One campaign per market, services as ad groups, SKAG treatment on the head terms that clear your value threshold, Performance Max layered in only after Search generates clean conversion data — and a budget model that moves dollars toward marginal return instead of splitting spend evenly to keep the peace.

Run your account through the decision tree honestly. If your locations share one campaign, if your CPL is a blended number, or if PMax launched before your conversion tracking could tell a qualified call from a wrong number, the account has margin trapped inside it. Restructuring is unglamorous work, but it's the difference between an account that spends and an account that scales.

faq.question: Should each location have its own Google Ads account or just its own campaign?
faq.answer: Own campaign, same account — almost always. Separate accounts fragment conversion data, multiply admin overhead, and prevent shared negative lists and portfolio bidding. The exceptions are franchise systems where each owner pays from their own card and needs billing isolation, or where a franchisor mandates separation. Even then, run everything under one MCC (manager account) so you keep cross-account visibility and shared audiences.

faq.question: How much budget does each location need for Smart Bidding to work?
faq.answer: Target roughly 30 conversions per month per campaign for Target CPA to stabilize. In most home-service categories with $40–$90 CPLs, that means $1,500–$2,500 per location per month as a floor. Below that, don't force automation — run Maximize Clicks with a max CPC cap, tight geo and keyword targeting, and manual weekly reviews until conversion volume justifies the switch.

faq.question: Is Performance Max better than Search for local service businesses?
faq.answer: No — it's complementary, not superior. Search captures declared, high-intent demand and gives you query-level control. PMax extends reach into Maps, YouTube, and Display, typically adding 15–25% incremental leads at a higher CPL. Run Search first, feed it 90 days of qualified conversion data, then layer PMax per major market. Launching PMax without clean conversion tracking teaches it to chase junk leads.

faq.question: What if two locations serve overlapping territory?
faq.answer: Cluster them into one metro campaign and split coverage at the ad-group or radius level instead of running two campaigns that bid against each other's geography. Assign ZIP codes to each location based on drive time and job history, use location-specific landing pages and tracking numbers for attribution, and route leads by ZIP in your CRM. Overlapping campaigns in the same auction inflate your own CPCs.

faq.question: How long does a restructure take to show results?
faq.answer: Expect two to four weeks of Smart Bidding relearning after a significant restructure — performance often dips slightly before improving. Preserve conversion history where possible by editing existing campaigns rather than deleting and rebuilding. Most accounts see per-location CPL clarity immediately, meaningful efficiency gains by week six, and the full benefit once offline conversion data starts feeding value-based bidding around the 90-day mark.

articles.title: How to Structure Google Ads Campaigns for Multi-Location Service Businesses
articles.description: A media buyer's decision tree for structuring Google Ads across multiple service locations. SKAGs vs PMax, geo-targeting, and budget thresholds that actually work.
articles.keyword: how to structure google ads campaigns for multi location service businesses
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most multi-location service businesses are lighting money on fire with a single national campaign and "location extensions." I've audited 40+ accounts running plumbing, HVAC, dental, legal, and lending shops across 3-25 locations, and the pattern is identical: one bloated campaign, mixed geo signals, wasted spend on cities that don't convert, and no visibility into which market is actually profitable. This guide is for founders, CMOs, and agency owners running paid search for service businesses with 2+ physical locations or service areas. If you're spending between $5K and $250K/month across markets and can't tell me your cost-per-booked-job by city, this is for you. Below: the exact campaign architecture decision tree we use, when single keyword ad groups (SKAGs) beat Performance Max, when PMax actually wins, and the budget thresholds that determine which approach makes sense.

Why a single national campaign fails multi-location businesses

The default Google Ads setup — one campaign, one ad group per service, location extensions bolted on — breaks the moment you cross two markets. Here's why. Bid landscapes differ dramatically by geo. A "emergency plumber" click in Phoenix might cost $32; in Tulsa it's $11. Lump them together and Google's Smart Bidding averages the signal, overpaying in cheap markets and underbidding in expensive ones. Your CPA looks fine on the dashboard while individual markets bleed. Conversion rates also swing wildly by location — driven by local competition, brand awareness, and even review counts on your GBP. Miami might convert at 8%, Jacksonville at 22%. A blended campaign treats them the same. Then there's the reporting problem. When your CFO asks "should we double down in Austin or pull back?" you need clean per-market P&L. A single-campaign structure with location extensions gives you a geo report inside Google Ads, but it doesn't let you set independent budgets, bid strategies, or ad copy per city. You end up making capital allocation decisions on averaged data. Rule of thumb: if a market represents more than 10% of your spend or revenue, it deserves its own campaign. Full stop.

The three architectures to choose between

For multi-location service businesses, you have three viable structures. Everything else is a variation. 1. Geo-segmented Search campaigns with SKAGs (or STAGs) One Search campaign per city (or metro), with tightly themed ad groups — often single keyword ad groups or single theme ad groups. Best for high-intent bottom-funnel keywords like "emergency AC repair Denver" or "bankruptcy attorney Tampa." 2. Performance Max per location group A PMax campaign scoped to a specific geo, feeding location-specific assets and audience signals. Best when you have solid conversion volume (30+ conversions/month per campaign) and want to capture demand across Search, Maps, YouTube, Discover, and Display. 3. Hybrid: Search for bottom-funnel + PMax for coverage Search campaigns own the money keywords per city. PMax handles broader intent and long-tail. Requires negative keyword hygiene between them and account-level negative keyword lists (which PMax finally supports). The wrong question is "SKAG or PMax?" The right question is "how many locations, what's my budget per location, and how much conversion data do I have per market?" That's what the decision tree below solves for.

The decision tree: locations x budget x conversion volume

Here's the framework I use in every account audit. Answer these three questions in order. Step 1: How many locations?

  • 2-5 locations: geo-segmented Search campaigns are almost always right.
  • 6-15 locations: hybrid, grouped by DMA or metro.
  • 16+ locations: PMax with location asset groups, plus Search for your top 5 revenue markets. Step 2: What's your monthly budget per location?
  • Under $2K/location: consolidate — you don't have the volume to feed Smart Bidding per campaign. Use one Search campaign with geo bid adjustments or ad group-level targeting.
  • $2K-$8K/location: geo-segmented Search with SKAGs. Manual CPC or Maximize Conversions with tCPA cap once you hit 15 conversions/month per campaign.
  • $8K-$25K/location: hybrid — Search for money terms, PMax for coverage.
  • $25K+/location: full hybrid plus a separate brand campaign, competitor conquest campaign, and PMax with retail-style asset groups. Step 3: Conversions per location per month?
  • Under 15: Smart Bidding is unreliable. Stick to manual or Maximize Clicks with tight negatives.
  • 15-30: Maximize Conversions is fine; tCPA is aspirational.
  • 30+: tCPA or tROAS becomes viable per campaign. If you fail the volume test, either consolidate campaigns or hold the line on manual bidding. Do not let Google's rep talk you into PMax with 8 conversions/month — you'll pay for the learning.

When geo-targeted SKAGs still win in 2026

SKAGs are supposedly dead. In multi-location Search, they're not — they've just evolved into single-theme ad groups (STAGs) because of close variants. Here's when they still print money. High-CPC emergency services. "Emergency plumber near me," "24 hour locksmith," "same day HVAC repair." Clicks cost $25-$80. You cannot afford a fuzzy match. One tightly-themed ad group per intent per city with phrase and exact match, RSAs pinned to the city name in headline 1, and a dedicated landing page = the highest converting structure I've ever run. Regulated verticals. Legal, lending, medical. Ad copy compliance changes by state. Separate campaigns per state let you tailor disclaimers, adjust for state-specific Quality Score patterns, and pause instantly if a compliance issue hits. Markets where you're outbid but need presence. In a city where you're #4 in ad rank, a broad PMax will chase impressions and waste spend. A tight SKAG structure lets you dominate 3-4 money terms profitably and skip the rest. Use Optmyzr or Adalysis for n-gram analysis and search term mining if you're running 10+ SKAG-style campaigns. Manual management above that scale is masochism.

When Performance Max is actually the right call

PMax gets trashed by every performance marketer with a Twitter account, but it works — under specific conditions. You have strong first-party conversion data. Not form fills. Booked appointments, qualified leads, or revenue pushed back to Google via offline conversion imports or the Enhanced Conversions API. PMax with garbage signals produces garbage. PMax with revenue-weighted conversions and value rules per location is a different animal. You have 30+ conversions per campaign per month. Below this, the algorithm doesn't learn — it hallucinates. You've done the negative work. Account-level negative keyword lists (rolled out in 2024), brand exclusions, and account-level placement exclusions must be locked down before you launch. Otherwise PMax will spend 40% of budget on YouTube kids' content and mobile app placements. Structure PMax by location group. Don't run one national PMax with location assets — run one PMax per DMA or region with:

  • Asset group per service line
  • Location-specific images and video
  • Audience signals built from your CRM (upload converters by geo)
  • Final URL expansion off until you trust the landing page coverage For multi-location home services, we've seen PMax pull 30-45% lower CPA than Search alone — but only after 60 days of tuning and only when Search is running in parallel to protect the money keywords.

Conversion tracking that actually supports this structure

None of this architecture matters if your tracking is broken. Here's the stack that supports multi-location decision-making. Server-side tagging via GTM Server. Client-side pixels are getting eaten by ITP, ad blockers, and iOS. Server-side gives you cleaner attribution and better Enhanced Conversions match rates. Offline conversion imports. Web leads are noisy. What you actually care about is booked jobs, closed loans, retained clients. Pipe your CRM (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, Salesforce) back to Google Ads via the Google Ads API or a middleware like Zapier/Make. Include the GCLID at form submission, tag the lead status downstream, and push "booked" or "revenue" events back within 14 days. Value rules per location. In Google Ads, set conversion value rules so a lead from a high-margin market (say, Denver) is worth $180 and a lead from a low-margin market is $80. Smart Bidding will optimize accordingly. Per-location call tracking. CallRail or WhatConverts with dynamic number insertion, tagged by campaign and landing page. Route calls to the right branch, but attribute revenue back to the campaign that produced them. A dashboard your CFO trusts. Looker Studio pulling from Google Ads, GA4, and your CRM, sliced by location. If you can't show cost-per-booked-job by city in one view, you can't make allocation decisions.

Implementation roadmap: first 30-60-90 days

Rebuilding an account is a project. Here's the sequence that keeps revenue stable during the migration. Days 1-14: audit and instrument.

  • Pull geo report for the last 90 days. Rank locations by spend, conversions, and revenue.
  • Fix tracking first: server-side GTM, offline conversion imports, call tracking DNI.
  • Build the negative keyword lists at account level.
  • Map each location to a bucket in the decision tree above. Days 15-30: build in parallel.
  • Launch new geo-segmented campaigns in paused state.
  • Build location-specific landing pages (page per city, not a template swap — real local proof, real reviews, real photos).
  • Copy top-performing search terms into new SKAG/STAG structure.
  • Set up conversion value rules per location. Days 31-45: shift traffic gradually.
  • Cap old campaign budgets by 25% per week.
  • Bring new campaigns live at 50% target budget.
  • Watch impression share and CPA daily. Adjust bids manually for the first two weeks. Days 46-90: layer and optimize.
  • Once Search campaigns have 15+ conversions/campaign/month, layer PMax by DMA if the budget supports it.
  • Turn on Smart Bidding (Maximize Conversions with tCPA) once volume supports it.
  • Kill the old campaigns.
  • Weekly review: n-gram analysis, geo bid adjustments, landing page CVR by city. Expect a 10-20% dip in weeks 3-5 as new campaigns exit learning. Budget for it. On the other side, we typically see 25-40% CPA reduction and clean per-market P&L within 90 days.

The bottom line

There is no universal "best" structure for multi-location service Google Ads accounts. There is a decision tree: how many locations, how much budget per location, how many conversions per location per month. Run that math, pick the architecture, and stop letting a Google rep dictate your structure based on their quarterly PMax quota. If you take one thing from this: any market worth more than 10% of your spend deserves its own campaign, its own budget, and its own landing page. Blended reporting hides blended waste. Rebuild once, instrument properly, and you'll be making capital allocation decisions on data instead of vibes.

faq.question: Should I use one Google Ads account for all locations or separate accounts?
faq.answer: One account with multiple campaigns, unless you have 25+ locations under separate legal entities or franchisees managing their own budgets. Separate accounts fragment your conversion data, hurt Smart Bidding learning, and multiply management overhead. Use campaign-level segmentation, not account-level.

faq.question: How many conversions do I need before switching from manual bidding to Smart Bidding?
faq.answer: At the campaign level, 15 conversions per month is the floor for Maximize Conversions, 30+ for tCPA, and 50+ for tROAS. Below 15, Smart Bidding will produce erratic CPAs because the algorithm doesn't have enough signal to model. Stay manual or use Maximize Clicks with tight negatives until you clear that bar.

faq.question: Can Performance Max replace my Search campaigns entirely?
faq.answer: No, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise. PMax cannibalizes brand and high-intent Search terms if you let it. Run Search campaigns for your money keywords and brand, then use PMax for coverage on broader intent. Add your brand and top converting exact-match terms as account-level negatives on PMax where possible.

faq.question: How do I handle a service area business without a physical storefront in each city?
faq.answer: Use location targeting set to "presence or interest" with the service area radius, and be explicit in ad copy and landing pages about which cities you serve. Do not use Google Business Profile location assets unless you have a real address there — service area businesses should rely on structured location targeting plus city-specific landing pages.

faq.question: What's the minimum budget to make geo-segmented campaigns worth it?
faq.answer: About $2,000/month per location. Below that, you won't generate enough conversions per campaign to feed Smart Bidding or make statistically meaningful decisions. Consolidate low-budget markets into a single regional campaign with geo bid adjustments until they scale.

articles.title: Google Ads for Window Replacement Contractors: Cost Per Lead
articles.description: Real cost-per-lead benchmarks for window replacement Google Ads — $85 to $220 by market size — plus keyword bid data and landing page fixes that cut CPL.
articles.keyword: meta ads for personal injury law firms
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
A qualified window replacement lead from Google Ads costs between $85 and $220 in most US markets right now. If you're paying more than that, the problem is almost never Google's auction — it's your keyword list, your landing page, or what happens in the five minutes after the form gets submitted.

Those numbers aren't theoretical. They come from patterns across 40+ home services and contractor accounts, where the same variables show up again and again: search intent tiering, negative keyword discipline, and landing page conversion rate. Window replacement is one of the highest-ticket residential services you can advertise — a full-house job runs $12,000 to $25,000 — which means the auction is expensive, but the math still works beautifully when the funnel is built right.

Here's exactly what leads cost, why they cost that, and where the money leaks out.

What a window replacement lead actually costs by market size

Cost per lead for window replacement search campaigns clusters into three bands:

  • Major metros (Dallas, Phoenix, Chicago, Atlanta): $150–$220 per lead. CPCs run $14–$28 on high-intent terms, and you're bidding against Renewal by Andersen, Window World, and two dozen PE-backed roll-ups with in-house media teams.
  • Mid-size markets (San Antonio, Tucson, Oklahoma City, Louisville): $110–$160 per lead. CPCs of $9–$18, thinner franchise competition, and homeowners who still search the same way.
  • Small metros and secondary markets: $85–$120 per lead. CPCs of $6–$12, and often only two or three serious advertisers in the auction.

Two caveats matter. First, these are form fill or call leads — not booked appointments. A booked in-home consultation typically costs 1.6x–2x the raw CPL once you account for no-shows and unqualified inquiries. Second, seasonality moves these bands 20–30%. Spring and early fall are the expensive windows (pun intended); December and January are when smart contractors keep spending because CPCs sag while competitors pause.

If your account is producing leads at $250+ in a mid-size market, don't accept 'it's a competitive industry' from your agency. Something specific is broken, and it's usually one of the next three sections.

The keyword bids driving your CPL

Window replacement keywords price according to intent, and the spread is dramatic. Roughly, the tiers look like this:

  • Buy-now intent: 'window replacement near me', 'window replacement companies [city]', 'replacement windows [city]' — $12–$28 per click in metros. These convert at 8–14% on a decent landing page.
  • Cost-research intent: 'window replacement cost', 'how much to replace windows', 'average cost of new windows' — $6–$12 per click. These convert at 3–6%, but the leads close slower because homeowners are still budgeting.
  • Product-research intent: 'vinyl vs fiberglass windows', 'best replacement window brands' — $3–$7 per click, sub-3% conversion. Skip these on lead gen budgets under $10K/month.

The mistake most contractor accounts make is bidding all three tiers into one campaign with one budget. Google's smart bidding then drifts spend toward the cheap clicks, your average CPC looks great in reporting, and your cost per booked appointment quietly doubles.

Separate campaigns by intent tier. Put 70% of budget on buy-now terms, 30% on cost-research terms with a financing-focused landing page ('new windows from $89/month' outperforms 'free quote' for this tier), and zero on product research until you have retargeting in place to catch them later.

The search terms quietly burning 20 to 35 percent of your budget

Pull the search terms report on any unmanaged window replacement account and you'll find the same leaks. Across contractor audits, 20–35% of spend routinely goes to queries that will never become a job:

  • Auto glass: 'car window replacement', 'windshield', 'window regulator', 'power window motor'. Broad match loves these because the click is cheap.
  • Repair-only intent: 'window glass repair', 'foggy glass fix', 'screen replacement', 'broken seal repair'. Unless you sell repairs, these are dead spend — and even if you do, they deserve their own campaign at their own CPL target.
  • DIY and parts: 'window replacement parts', 'how to replace a window yourself', 'sash kit', 'Home Depot windows'.
  • Renters and commercial mismatches: 'apartment window', 'storefront glass' — depending on your service mix.

Build a negative keyword list of 150–300 terms before launch, not after the first $3,000 teaches you the hard way. Then review the search terms report weekly for the first 60 days.

This is the single fastest CPL fix available. Cutting 25% waste doesn't just save the money — it feeds Google's bidding algorithm cleaner conversion data, which compounds. Accounts that fix negatives typically see CPL drop 30–40% within six weeks without touching anything else.

Landing page benchmarks: where $150 clicks go to die

The auction sets your click price. Your landing page sets your lead price. Same traffic, different pages, wildly different economics:

  • Sub-5% conversion rate: something is structurally wrong. At $15 CPC, you're paying $300+ per lead.
  • 8–12%: the healthy range for window replacement. This is where the $85–$220 CPL bands live.
  • 15%+: achievable with a strong financing offer, aggressive social proof, and a market where you have real brand recognition.

What the 10%+ pages have in common:

  1. A financing-led headline. 'New Windows From $89/Month — Free In-Home Quote' beats 'Quality Window Installation Since 1998' every single time. Homeowners think in monthly payments on five-figure purchases.
  2. A two-step quote form. Step one asks how many windows — a zero-commitment question. Step two captures contact info. Two-step forms lift conversion 20–40% over single-step in nearly every contractor test.
  3. Click-to-call above the fold on mobile, where 65–75% of this traffic lives.
  4. Before/after photos of local jobs — real houses, real addresses' neighborhoods, not stock imagery.
  5. Review count and rating pulled from Google — '4.9 stars across 312 local reviews' does more than any paragraph of copy.

Sending Google Ads traffic to your homepage instead of a dedicated page like this is the most expensive lazy decision in contractor marketing. It alone can double your CPL.

Local Services Ads vs Search: run both, but know the difference

Google Local Services Ads (LSAs) sit above regular search ads, charge per lead instead of per click, and for window contractors typically price at $45–$95 per lead depending on market. So why run Search campaigns at all?

Because LSAs have three hard limits. Volume caps — LSA lead flow is throttled by your review count, response rate, and Google's rotation; you can't scale it by raising budget the way you can with Search. No message control — you can't test offers, financing hooks, or landing pages; you're a name, a rating, and a checkmark. Dispute overhead — a meaningful share of LSA leads are wrong-service or spam calls, and clawing back credits takes discipline most contractors don't have.

The right structure for most window replacement companies:

  • LSAs on, fully verified, budget uncapped — take every lead Google will give you at that price. It's usually your cheapest source, just not your biggest.
  • Search campaigns as the volume engine — this is where budget scales and where your offer differentiates you.
  • Performance Max only after Search has 60+ days of clean conversion data to feed it. PMax launched on an empty account chases junk conversions and inflates reported results while the phone stays quiet.

Contractors who run LSA-only plateau at 15–25 leads a month in most markets. The Search + LSA combination is what gets you to 60+.

Speed-to-lead: the CPL multiplier nobody puts in the ad account

Here's the uncomfortable math: a $150 lead that gets a callback in five minutes and a $150 lead that gets a callback in four hours are not the same asset. Harvard Business Review's classic response study found contact rates drop roughly 8x between the 5-minute and 30-minute mark, and contractor data bears it out — homeowners requesting window quotes typically submit to 2–3 companies in one sitting. First voice on the phone frames the entire comparison.

If you're spending $5,000/month on ads and responding to leads 'when the office gets to it', your effective cost per booked appointment can be double what your ad account reports. The fix is automation, not heroics:

  • Instant SMS on form submit via GoHighLevel or similar — 'Thanks [name], this is [company]. Quick question so we quote you accurately: roughly how many windows?' A question, not a confirmation. Questions get replies.
  • Missed-call text back for every unanswered inbound call.
  • AI voice or answering coverage for nights and weekends — 35–40% of contractor form fills happen outside business hours, and they're often the highest-intent ones (homeowners researching after dinner).
  • A 5-touch follow-up sequence over 10 days for leads that don't book immediately. Roughly a third of booked window appointments come from follow-up touches, not the first response.

Before you blame Google for expensive leads, audit your median response time. It's the cheapest CPL lever you own.

The budget math: what it takes to make this profitable

Work backwards from the job, not forwards from the click.

Assume a mid-size market: $130 average CPL, and an average job value of $14,000 on full or partial house replacements. A realistic mid-funnel looks like: 55% of leads become sat appointments, and 30% of sat appointments close. That's a 16.5% lead-to-sale rate — one job per six leads, or roughly $790 in ad cost per closed job.

On a $14,000 job at 45% gross margin, you're generating $6,300 in gross profit against $790 of media — an 8:1 return before agency fees. That is why the auction is expensive: the math is good, and everyone bidding knows it.

What that means for budget planning:

  • $3,000/month buys roughly 20–25 leads → 3–4 jobs/month. Viable for a crew or two, but volatile — one bad week distorts the whole month.
  • $5,000–$8,000/month is the stability zone: 40–60 leads, 7–10 jobs, enough conversion volume for smart bidding to actually optimize.
  • $10,000+/month is where you're capacity-constrained before you're demand-constrained, and installation scheduling becomes the bottleneck.

Give any new account 90 days before judging it. Month one is data acquisition, month two is optimization, month three is what the account will actually do. Contractors who pull the plug at week five are paying for the expensive part and leaving before the cheap part starts.

The bottom line

The contractors winning on Google Ads in window replacement aren't the ones with the biggest budgets — they're the ones with the tightest funnels. An $85–$220 CPL is the market rate for a qualified lead, and every dollar above that range traces back to a fixable cause: mixed-intent campaigns, missing negatives, homepage traffic, or slow follow-up.

Audit those four things in that order. Most accounts we open up have at least two of them broken, and fixing them changes the economics of the entire channel — same spend, same market, double the jobs.

faq.question: What is a good cost per lead for window replacement Google Ads?
faq.answer: In most US markets, $85–$220 per raw lead is the healthy range — $85–$120 in small metros, $110–$160 in mid-size markets, and $150–$220 in major metros against national franchise competition. A booked in-home appointment typically costs 1.6x–2x the raw lead cost. If you're consistently above $250 in a mid-size market, look at negative keywords, landing page conversion rate, and intent mixing before blaming competition.

faq.question: How much should a window replacement contractor budget for Google Ads per month?
faq.answer: The stability zone is $5,000–$8,000/month, which produces roughly 40–60 leads and 7–10 closed jobs in a typical mid-size market. You can start at $3,000/month and get 3–4 jobs, but expect volatility — the account has less conversion data for smart bidding to learn from. Plan for a full 90 days before judging performance; months one and two are data acquisition and optimization.

faq.question: Are Google Local Services Ads better than Search ads for window companies?
faq.answer: LSAs are usually cheaper per lead ($45–$95) but they cap out — volume is throttled by your reviews and responsiveness, not your budget, and you can't test offers or landing pages. Search campaigns cost more per lead but scale with spend and let you differentiate with financing offers. Run both: LSAs uncapped as your cheapest source, Search as your volume engine. LSA-only accounts typically plateau around 15–25 leads a month.

faq.question: Why is my cost per lead so high for window replacement ads?
faq.answer: Four causes account for almost every inflated CPL: auto-glass and repair queries eating budget (check your search terms report — 20–35% waste is common without negatives), mixing buy-now and research keywords in one campaign, sending traffic to your homepage instead of a dedicated landing page with a financing offer and two-step form, and slow lead response. Fixing negative keywords alone typically drops CPL 30–40% within six weeks.

faq.question: Do financing offers really improve window replacement ad performance?
faq.answer: Yes — it's consistently the highest-impact offer test for this vertical. Homeowners evaluate five-figure purchases in monthly payments, so 'New Windows From $89/Month' outperforms 'Free Estimate' headlines on both click-through and landing page conversion, especially for cost-research keywords. Pair the financing hook with a two-step quote form and you're stacking the two biggest conversion levers in the vertical.

articles.title: Google Ads for Window Replacement Contractors: Real CPL Data
articles.description: Cost per lead benchmarks for window replacement Google Ads ($85-$220), keyword bids by market, and landing page conversion data from 40+ contractor campaigns.
articles.keyword: google ads for window replacement contractors cost per lead
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Here's what most window replacement contractors won't tell you: if your Google Ads cost per lead is under $85, you're either running in a rural market with zero competition or you're counting form spam as leads. If it's over $220, you're getting hosed by your agency or your landing page is broken. This breakdown is for window replacement contractors, remodeling company owners, and the media buyers running their accounts. Not theory — actual CPL ranges, keyword-level bid data, and landing page conversion benchmarks pulled from 40+ contractor Google Ads accounts we've audited or managed across tier-1, tier-2, and tier-3 U.S. metros. By the end, you'll know what a realistic CPL looks like in your market, which keywords are worth bidding on, and the conversion rate your landing page needs to hit to make the math work.

The realistic CPL range: $85 to $220 (and why yours might be higher)

Across the window replacement accounts we've touched, cost per lead lands between $85 and $220 on Google Search. That's a wide spread, and market size explains most of it. Here's the breakdown by metro tier: - Tier-1 metros (NYC, LA, Chicago, Boston, DC, SF Bay): $165–$220 CPL. High CPCs, aggressive competitors like Renewal by Andersen and Champion, and expensive geo-targeting.

  • Tier-2 metros (Charlotte, Nashville, Kansas City, Indianapolis, Tampa): $110–$160 CPL. This is the sweet spot — meaningful demand without the CPC bloodbath.
  • Tier-3 markets (secondary cities, exurbs): $85–$120 CPL. Cheaper clicks, but lower search volume means you'll cap out on scale fast. If you're seeing CPLs above $250, one of three things is happening: you're bidding on broad match without negatives, your landing page is converting under 6%, or your Quality Score is dragging your CPCs up 30-40%. Pull your search terms report from the last 30 days. If you see queries like "window cleaning" or "window tint" showing spend, that's your first fix. CPL is a downstream metric. It's CPC × conversion rate, nothing more. Fix either lever and CPL moves.

Keyword bid data: what you're actually paying per click

The CPC data below is pulled from active window replacement campaigns, not Google Keyword Planner estimates (which lie). These are top-of-page bid ranges we've observed: - "window replacement [city]" — $18–$42 CPC. High intent, high competition. This is your money keyword.

  • "replacement windows near me" — $22–$48 CPC. Even more expensive because Home Advisor and Angi bid aggressively.
  • "vinyl window replacement" — $14–$28 CPC. Slightly lower intent, better margins.
  • "double hung window installation" — $9–$18 CPC. Product-specific, converts well.
  • "window replacement cost" — $6–$14 CPC. Research-stage. Convert at 3-5% unless you have a strong cost calculator.
  • "cheap windows" / "discount windows" — $4–$9 CPC. Skip these. Wrong customer profile. Tactical move: run separate campaigns for branded manufacturer terms ("Pella replacement," "Andersen 400 series install"). CPCs drop to $5–$12 and lead quality is significantly higher because searchers already know what they want. Use phrase and exact match only in this vertical. Broad match with Smart Bidding sounds good in a Google rep pitch but burns budget on "window AC" and "car window" queries in real accounts. We've seen 22-35% of broad match spend land on non-window intent queries in unaudited accounts.

Landing page conversion benchmarks from 40+ contractor campaigns

Your CPC is largely fixed by the auction. Your conversion rate is not. This is where CPL is actually won or lost. Here's what we see across contractor landing pages: - Generic homepage as landing page: 2-4% conversion rate. Don't do this.

  • Basic dedicated LP (hero, form, some copy): 6-8%.
  • Optimized LP (offer, social proof, trust signals, mobile-first form): 10-14%.
  • High-performing LP with instant quote calculator or financing hook: 15-22%. The difference between 4% and 12% conversion is 3x more leads at the same CPC. That's it. That's the whole game. What separates a 12%+ landing page from an 8% one: 1. Above-the-fold offer — "$1,500 off 5+ windows" or "0% financing for 60 months" — not "Quality windows since 1998"
  1. Two-step form — ZIP code first, then contact details. Increases starts by 40-60%.
  2. Local trust signals — real photos of local projects, license number visible, BBB rating, Google review count with screenshot
  3. Mobile load under 2.5 seconds — 68% of window replacement clicks are mobile. Run PageSpeed Insights. Every second above 3s costs you ~7% of conversions.
  4. Financing prominence — window jobs run $8K–$25K. Financing is often the actual buying decision. Build dedicated LPs in Unbounce, Instapage, or a stripped GoHighLevel funnel. Not on your WordPress site with a Contact Us form.

The math: what CPL you need to make Google Ads profitable

Before you obsess over hitting $95 CPL, know what CPL your unit economics can absorb. Work backwards. Assume typical window replacement numbers: - Average job size: $12,000

  • Gross margin: 35% = $4,200 gross profit
  • Lead-to-appointment rate: 55%
  • Appointment-to-sale rate: 30%
  • Lead-to-sale rate: ~16.5% That means 1 sale per ~6 leads. If you want customer acquisition cost at 20% of gross profit ($840), your target CPL is: $840 ÷ 6 leads = $140 max CPL If your CPL is $180 in a tier-1 market, you're at 26% CAC-to-GP — still workable but tight. If it's $95 in a tier-3 market, you're at 14% — highly profitable, scale it. The founders who lose money on Google Ads almost always have one of these problems: appointment set rate under 40% (broken speed-to-lead), close rate under 20% (weak sales process), or average ticket under $8K (wrong customer profile from broad keywords). Google Ads is rarely the problem. The funnel around it usually is. Track lead-to-sale by keyword in a CRM like HubSpot or GoHighLevel and you'll spot which campaigns are actually profitable versus just "cheap."

Speed-to-lead: the hidden CPL multiplier

Two contractors bid on the same keywords, run the same landing page, and hit the same $130 CPL. One does $2M in revenue from Google Ads. The other does $600K. The difference is almost always speed-to-lead. InMoment and Velocify data (backed by what we see in accounts) shows contact rate drops off a cliff after 5 minutes: - Called within 1 minute: 78% contact rate

  • Called within 5 minutes: 62%
  • Called within 30 minutes: 36%
  • Called after 1 hour: 21% If you're closing 30% of appointments and only contacting 36% of leads, your effective CPL just tripled. That $130 lead cost is really $360 per contactable lead. Fix stack: 1. Instant lead notification via GoHighLevel, Zapier, or CallRail to a shared SMS/Slack channel
  1. Auto-text within 60 seconds: "Hey [name], this is Mike from [Company]. Saw you're looking at windows for your [city] home. What's a good time to talk today?"
  2. Auto-dial workflow — 3 call attempts in the first hour, then day 1, day 2, day 4
  3. After-hours coverage — 22% of window replacement leads come in between 7pm–11pm. If you don't cover this, you're throwing away 20%+ of paid spend. AI voice agents (Air.ai, Synthflow) are increasingly viable here — imperfect but better than a lead sitting until 8am.

Campaign structure that actually works for window contractors

Most contractor accounts are structured wrong. Either everything is dumped into one campaign, or there are 40 ad groups nobody manages. Here's the structure that consistently delivers $100–$150 CPL in tier-2 markets: Campaign 1: Core Window Replacement — Exact + Phrase

  • Ad groups by intent: "replacement," "installation," "new windows"
  • Manual CPC or Target CPA (only after 30+ conversions)
  • Geo-targeted to your service radius, not statewide Campaign 2: Product-Specific
  • Ad groups by window type: double-hung, casement, bay, sliding
  • Lower CPCs, higher intent buyers Campaign 3: Manufacturer Brand Terms
  • Pella, Andersen, Marvin, Milgard (whichever you sell)
  • Cheapest CPCs in the account Campaign 4: Competitor Conquesting (optional)
  • Bid on "Renewal by Andersen reviews," "Champion windows cost"
  • Higher CPL but often steals late-stage buyers Campaign 5: Local Service Ads (LSA)
  • Not technically Google Ads, but run it. LSA CPL for window contractors is typically $65–$140 and leads come pre-qualified. Negative keyword list from day one: cleaning, tint, screen, repair (unless you offer it), AC, car, storm, DIY, cheap, wholesale, commercial, Home Depot, Lowe's, Menards, replacement glass, broken. Check search terms weekly for the first 90 days. This is where most budget gets saved.

Tracking that actually reflects reality

Contractors routinely think their CPL is $95 when it's actually $180 because they're counting form fills, calls under 30 seconds, and duplicate submissions as "leads." Fix the tracking before optimizing anything. Minimum stack: - CallRail or CallTrackingMetrics — dynamic number insertion, only count calls over 60 seconds as conversions

  • GA4 with conversion events firing on qualified form submits (spam-filtered)
  • CRM integration (HubSpot, GoHighLevel, JobNimbus) — push lead status back so you can see cost-per-appointment and cost-per-sale by campaign
  • Google Ads offline conversion imports — feed appointment and sale data back to Google so Smart Bidding optimizes for revenue, not form fills The last one is the difference between a mediocre account and a great one. When Google's algorithm learns which leads actually turn into $15K jobs, tCPA campaigns start finding buyers instead of tire-kickers. Expect 20-35% CPL improvement over 60-90 days after offline conversion import goes live. Also: build a spam filter on your forms. reCAPTCHA v3, honeypot fields, and blocking VPN/proxy IPs will cut junk leads by 15-25% in most contractor accounts. That's a direct CPL reduction because you're not paying for fake conversions.

What to do in your first 30 days if you're starting fresh

If you're launching Google Ads for a window replacement business or resetting a broken account, here's the sequence: 1. Week 1: Build one dedicated landing page with a real offer, financing callout, and two-step form. Set up CallRail and GA4 conversion tracking. Load a 200+ negative keyword list. 2. Week 2: Launch one campaign, exact match only, 5-8 keywords, $150-$300/day budget, manual CPC starting at market rate. Target your top 3 service ZIPs only. 3. Week 3: Add phrase match variants. Layer in RSAs with 3 headlines that reference your offer, financing, and local trust. Start LSA in parallel. 4. Week 4: Review search terms daily. Add negatives aggressively. Once you hit 30+ conversions, consider switching to Maximize Conversions with a tCPA cap 20% above current CPL. What NOT to do in month one: Performance Max, broad match with Smart Bidding, display network, YouTube. All will burn cash before you have conversion data to steer them. Expect month one CPL to be 30-50% higher than your steady state. The algorithm is learning, you're learning the search terms, and your LP is unoptimized. By month three, if you've done the work, you should be inside the $85-$220 band for your market tier. If not, the problem is almost always the landing page or the offer, not the ad platform.

The bottom line
