Crucially, treat shared leads as a speed contest: first contractor to a live conversation wins a disproportionate share, so automate an instant text-back and call within two minutes of every lead drop.

Phase 2 (months 3–4): Shift budget as the exclusive funnel proves out. When your funnel's cost per signed job beats the shared platform's for two consecutive months — and it usually does by month two — move 70–80% of spend to your own ads. Keep a small shared-lead budget only if the platform fills a specific gap, like a service area your ads haven't penetrated.

Phase 3 (ongoing): Exclusive funnel becomes the engine; shared platforms become surge capacity for slow weeks or new crews that need feeding. You set the dial instead of the platform setting it for you.

The destination is a pipeline where the majority of jobs come from assets you own — ads, audiences, reviews, referrals, and a database you can remarket to every spring. Shared platforms then become a tool you use opportunistically, not a landlord you pay indefinitely.

The bottom line

The shared-vs-exclusive debate ends the moment you measure cost per signed job instead of cost per lead. Shared leads sell the illusion of cheap volume; the auction dynamic quietly taxes your close rate and your pricing power on every deal. Exclusive funnels cost more per name and dramatically less per job — and every dollar builds an asset you keep.

The honest answer isn't ideology, it's a threshold: under ~$1,500/month in lead spend, rent volume from the platforms and win on speed. Above it, the math says own your funnel — because at that point, staying on shared leads is the most expensive decision on your marketing P&L.

faq.question: Are shared leads ever worth buying for contractors?
faq.answer: Yes, in two situations: when your total lead budget is under roughly $1,500/month (too thin to feed your own ad funnel properly), and as surge capacity to fill slow weeks or feed a new crew. In both cases, win by being first — automate an instant text-back and call within two minutes, because on shared leads the fastest responder takes a disproportionate share of the jobs.

faq.question: What close rate should I expect from exclusive leads?
faq.answer: With a solid offer, fast follow-up, and a real sales process, 25–40% of contacted exclusive leads is a realistic range for most trades, which typically nets out to 20–30% of all leads purchased. If you're closing under 10–15% on exclusive leads, the lead source usually isn't the problem — audit your speed-to-lead, your estimate presentation, and your follow-up sequence first.

faq.question: How much does it cost to build an exclusive lead funnel?
faq.answer: Plan on $1,000–$3,000 one-time for a landing page and offer build (less if you DIY in GoHighLevel), $97–$297/month for a CRM with automated follow-up, and either your own time or $1,000–$2,500/month for ad management. Ad spend is separate — $1,500–$5,000/month is the productive range for most local contractors. At typical margins the funnel pays for itself within the first one to two months.

faq.question: Why are my HomeAdvisor leads so hard to reach?
faq.answer: Because you're one of three to five contractors who bought the same homeowner, and they stop answering after the first couple of calls. Contact rates on shared leads commonly sit around 40–60%, versus 70–85% on exclusive leads called within five minutes. It's not your phone skills — it's the auction structure of the platform.

faq.question: Should I use Google or Meta ads for exclusive contractor leads?
faq.answer: Both, with different jobs. Google (Search and Local Services Ads) captures homeowners actively looking — higher cost per lead, higher intent, fastest close cycles. Meta generates demand at lower cost per lead with offer-led creative, ideal for big-ticket projects homeowners plan slowly, like roofs and remodels. Most contractors get the best blended cost per job running Google for capture and Meta for volume and retargeting.

articles.title: Exclusive Leads vs Shared Leads for Contractors: The Real Math
articles.description: The actual close-rate and CAC math on HomeAdvisor shared leads vs your own exclusive funnel — plus the exact break-even spend to run in-house.
articles.keyword: exclusive leads vs shared leads for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Here's the uncomfortable truth most contractors won't say out loud: if you're closing 4-6% of your HomeAdvisor leads, you're not running a business — you're subsidizing Angi's stock price. And if you think switching to "exclusive leads" from a third-party vendor fixes it, you're about to pay 3x the price for a lead that still isn't really yours. This breakdown is for remodeling, roofing, HVAC, and solar contractors doing $500K-$10M in revenue who are tired of guessing which lead channel actually prints money. We're going to run the real close-rate math, side by side, at real market prices. By the end, you'll know the exact monthly ad spend where an owned exclusive funnel beats shared leads — and when it doesn't.

What "shared" and "exclusive" actually mean in 2026

Let's kill the marketing language first. Shared leads are what HomeAdvisor, Angi, Thumbtack, Networx, and Modernize sell you. A single homeowner form-fill gets resold to 3-5 contractors simultaneously. You're racing four other guys to the phone, and the homeowner already knows they'll get spammed for a week. Exclusive leads come in two flavors, and this is where contractors get burned: - Vendor-exclusive: A third party (CraftJack, Service Direct, some Angi Ads tiers) runs ads, then sells the lead to only you. Price: $80-$400 depending on trade. You don't own the ad account, the pixel data, or the audience.

  • Owned exclusive: You run your own Meta and Google ads into your own funnel (GoHighLevel, HubSpot, or a custom site). The lead hits your CRM in under 60 seconds. Nobody else gets it, ever. The difference between vendor-exclusive and owned-exclusive is roughly the difference between renting and owning a house. Both put a roof over your head. Only one builds equity.

The real close-rate math on HomeAdvisor shared leads

I've audited close rates across 40+ contractor accounts. Here's the honest distribution on HomeAdvisor/Angi shared leads: - Top 10% of operators: 8-12% close rate

  • Median: 4-6%
  • Bottom half: 1-3% Let's model a median roofing contractor buying 100 shared leads/month at $65 average CPL: - Spend: $6,500
  • Contacts made: ~55 (roughly 45% ghost you or were fake)
  • Appointments set: ~18
  • Sits: ~11
  • Sales: 5 (at 5% close on total leads)
  • Average ticket: $12,000
  • Revenue: $60,000
  • Cost per acquisition: $1,300
  • Ad-cost-to-revenue ratio: 10.8% On paper, that looks fine. But we haven't counted the credits you'll fight for (budget on 15% of leads being disputed), the sales rep hours burned on unqualified junk, or the fact that your Google reviews get hammered when you can't respond in 90 seconds. Real, fully-loaded CAC on shared leads is closer to $1,600-$1,900.

The real close-rate math on an owned exclusive funnel

Now the same roofer runs their own Meta + Google Local Services setup. Here's what a competently-built funnel produces in most metros: - Meta CPL (lead-form or landing page): $22-$55 for storm/roof niches

  • Google LSA CPL: $45-$95, but pre-qualified
  • Blended CPL: ~$40 Because the lead is exclusive and hits your CRM in under 60 seconds via a webhook to GoHighLevel or HubSpot, speed-to-lead crushes the shared-lead economics: - 100 leads at $40 blended = $4,000 spend
  • Contact rate: ~75% (you're first, not fifth)
  • Appointments: ~35
  • Sits: ~22
  • Sales: 11 (11% close rate — realistic when you're not competing on the same call)
  • Revenue: $132,000
  • CAC: $364
  • Ad-cost-to-revenue ratio: 3% Even if you cut those numbers by 30% for a first-90-days ramp, the owned funnel still lands around $520 CAC. That's 3-4x better than shared. The catch? You need infrastructure, and there's a break-even point below which it doesn't work.

The break-even spend where owned exclusive beats shared

Here's where most "just run your own ads" advice falls apart. An owned funnel has fixed costs that shared leads don't: - Meta/Google management (agency or in-house media buyer): $2,000-$5,000/mo

  • CRM + automation stack (GoHighLevel, Twilio, Calendly): $300-$600/mo
  • Landing page + creative refresh: $500-$1,500/mo amortized
  • Call tracking (CallRail): $75-$300/mo Fully loaded, you need roughly $3,500-$6,500/mo in overhead before a dollar of ad spend. Run the math: at $40 CPL and 11% close, every $1,000 in ad spend produces roughly $33,000 in revenue at $12K ticket. But you need to clear the fixed nut first. Break-even ad spend vs. buying shared leads: - Below $3,000/mo in ad spend: stay on shared leads. Overhead eats the margin.
  • $3,000-$6,000/mo: hybrid — run owned ads for high-intent keywords, backfill with shared leads.
  • $6,000+/mo in ad spend: go fully owned. This is where the CAC gap becomes real money — usually $40K-$80K/mo in saved acquisition cost at scale. If you're spending under $3K/mo on marketing total, HomeAdvisor is genuinely the right answer. Above $10K/mo total marketing budget, staying on shared leads is malpractice.

Why speed-to-lead is the whole game

The single biggest variable in shared vs exclusive isn't the lead source — it's response time. MIT and InsideSales data on 15,000 leads showed contacting inside 5 minutes makes you 21x more likely to qualify the lead than waiting 30 minutes. Most contractors respond to HomeAdvisor leads in 8-45 minutes. By then, three competitors already called. On an owned funnel with proper automation, you can hit these numbers: 1. Lead submits form → webhook fires to GoHighLevel in <2 seconds 2. Automated SMS + email sends in <10 seconds ("Hey [name], this is Mike with [company] — got your roof inquiry, calling you in 60 seconds") 3. Round-robin call assignment triggers rep's phone 4. If no answer in 5 minutes, auto-voicemail drop + second SMS 5. Booking link (Calendly or GHL native) embedded in every message This stack is what turns an 11% close rate into a 14-16% close rate. Contractors who won't build this infrastructure should stay on shared leads — because without speed-to-lead automation, exclusive leads perform barely better than shared.

The hidden cost of not owning your pixel data

Here's the argument nobody makes for owned exclusive that matters most at scale: audience data compounds. When HomeAdvisor sells you a lead, they keep the pixel data. Every roof-quote form-fill trains their Meta and Google algorithms, not yours. After 12 months of buying shared leads, you have zero owned audience assets. Run your own Meta Ads Manager account for 12 months, and you'll have: - 5,000-20,000 pixeled website visitors for retargeting

  • 500-2,000 form-fills as a custom audience (and their lookalikes at 1%, 2%, 3%)
  • Email/SMS list of every past lead for reactivation campaigns
  • CAC that drops 20-40% in year two purely from algorithmic learning I've watched roofing companies go from $85 CPL in month 3 to $32 CPL in month 14 on the same ad spend — because the pixel finally knew who to target. Shared leads never give you that curve. You pay the same $65 per lead in year five as you did in year one, and if Angi raises prices 15%, you eat it.

The hybrid model that actually works for most contractors

For most contractors doing $1M-$4M in revenue, the correct answer is not "pick one." It's a portfolio: 60% owned exclusive (Meta + Google LSA into GoHighLevel): This is your growth engine. Predictable CAC, compounding data. 25% Google LSA + SEO: Highest intent, lowest CAC once ranked. Slow to build but nearly free at maturity. 15% shared leads (Angi/HomeAdvisor): Use these as fill-in volume during slow weeks and as training reps for junior salespeople. Don't build the business on them. Set hard rules: - Cap shared-lead spend at 15% of marketing budget

  • Track CAC by source weekly in a single dashboard (Google Sheets is fine; don't overcomplicate)
  • Kill any channel where fully-loaded CAC exceeds 15% of average ticket for two consecutive months
  • Reinvest 100% of savings from lower CAC into more owned ad spend, not overhead The operators who win in this market aren't the ones with the biggest ad budgets — they're the ones who know their CAC by source to the dollar and reallocate ruthlessly every 30 days.

The bottom line

Shared leads aren't inherently bad — they're a cash-flow product for contractors who can't yet afford the infrastructure of an owned funnel. But if you're spending more than $6K/month on lead generation and still buying primarily shared leads, you're leaving $30K-$80K/month in acquisition savings on the table, plus giving away audience data that compounds against you every quarter. Run your own break-even math this week. Pull your last 90 days of HomeAdvisor spend, calculate your true CAC (including credits, ghosted leads, and sales rep hours), and compare it to what a $40 blended CPL at 11% close would produce at your average ticket. If the gap is more than $500 per acquisition, you already have your answer — build the owned funnel.

faq.question: How many HomeAdvisor leads do I need to close to break even?
faq.answer: At a $65 average CPL and $12K average ticket with typical 30-35% gross margins, you need to close roughly 1 in 20 leads (5%) just to break even on the lead cost alone — before overhead, labor, or credits. Anything below a 5% close rate on shared leads is losing money.

faq.question: Are exclusive leads from vendors like CraftJack or Service Direct worth it?
faq.answer: Better than shared, worse than owned. Vendor-exclusive leads typically run $150-$400 and close at 12-18%, so the math often works. But you're renting the pipeline — the vendor owns the pixel data, the ad account, and can raise prices or drop you at will. Use them as a bridge while you build an owned funnel, not a permanent solution.

faq.question: What's the minimum monthly budget to run my own exclusive lead funnel?
faq.answer: Roughly $6,500/month all-in: $3,500 in ad spend plus $3,000 in management, tech stack, and creative. Below that, fixed costs eat too much of the margin and you'll perform worse than buying shared leads. Above $10K/month total, owned funnels dominate on every metric.

faq.question: How fast do I need to respond to leads to actually close them?
faq.answer: Under 5 minutes, ideally under 60 seconds. Data across 15,000+ B2C leads shows contacting inside 5 minutes makes you 21x more likely to qualify than waiting 30 minutes. Automate SMS and email in your CRM (GoHighLevel or HubSpot) so the first touch fires in under 10 seconds — the human callback should follow inside 2 minutes.

faq.question: Can I run Meta ads for contractor leads myself, or do I need an agency?
faq.answer: You can, but expect a 90-120 day ramp where CPL will be 2-3x higher than a competent agency's. If your time is worth more than $150/hour running the business, hire a specialist. If you have 15+ hours a week and enjoy media buying, learn it yourself — the tools (Meta Ads Manager, GoHighLevel) are accessible.

articles.title: The Best Lead Generation Strategy for Solar Companies Now
articles.description: Door-knocking lists are dead math. Here's the 3-channel paid stack plus database reactivation solar companies use to hit sub-$80 qualified leads.
articles.keyword: how to get commercial roofing leads
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
The average solar company still pays canvassers $18–$25 an hour to knock 80 doors and set two appointments — one of which cancels. That's a $200+ cost per sat appointment before a single kilowatt is quoted. Meanwhile, the operators quietly winning residential solar right now are generating qualified, utility-bill-verified leads at $60–$80 through a paid media stack that most solar CEOs have never structured correctly.

The difference isn't budget. It's architecture. Solar has one of the highest-intent buyer pools in home services — homeowners staring at a $280 electric bill every month — and one of the worst-executed acquisition playbooks. Purchased aggregator leads get resold five times. Door programs collapse the moment your best closer quits. And most solar Meta campaigns are optimized for form fills, not funded installs.

This is the 3-channel system we build for solar clients: Meta for volume, Google for intent capture, and database reactivation for near-free pipeline — all feeding one speed-to-lead engine. Here's exactly how it works and what each piece should cost.

Why door-knocking economics no longer work

Run the actual math on a canvassing program. A rep at $20/hour plus mileage knocks roughly 80–100 doors per shift. Industry-average contact rate is 30–40%, and of those contacts, maybe 2–4% agree to an appointment. That's 1–2 sets per shift, with a 40–50% sit rate. Your true cost per sat appointment lands between $180 and $320 — before manager overhead, turnover, and the recruiting treadmill.

And it's getting worse, not better. Video doorbells changed the game: a growing share of 'knocks' now get screened before the door ever opens. Municipal solicitation permits are tightening in exactly the suburbs with the best roofs. And rep churn in door programs routinely exceeds 100% annually, which means you're perpetually paying tenured-rep wages for rookie-rep output.

None of this means field teams are worthless — a great closer in the home still converts. The problem is using $25/hour humans as your lead generation layer when paid media can put a pre-qualified homeowner with a verified utility bill on your calendar for a third of the cost. Door teams should close demand. They should not be the thing that creates it. Every solar company still treating canvassing as its primary acquisition channel is subsidizing an expensive habit with margin it will want back at scale.

Why purchased solar leads are even worse

The reflexive alternative — buying leads from aggregators — usually trades one bad model for a worse one. Aggregator solar leads run $40–$150 each, which looks comparable to self-generated until you understand what you're actually buying: a lead that was sold to three to five other installers, often generated by sweepstakes-adjacent creative ('The government will pay for your panels!') that attracts exactly the homeowner who can't qualify for financing.

The numbers tell the story. Shared aggregator leads typically contact at 30–40% and close at 2–5%. At $75 per lead and a 3% close rate, you're paying $2,500 in lead cost per installed deal — and racing four competitors' dialers to get there. Compare that to exclusive, self-generated leads from your own ad account: 60–80% contact rates when you call within five minutes, and close rates of 8–15% depending on your sales process.

There's also an asset problem. Every dollar spent with an aggregator builds their audience data, their pixel, their negotiating leverage. Every dollar spent in your own Meta and Google accounts builds seasoned pixels, custom audiences, and creative learnings you own forever. One of these compounds. The other is rent. Founders who think in terms of asset ownership stop buying shared leads the moment they see the pixel-equity argument laid out.

Channel 1: Meta ads built for qualification, not form fills

Meta is your volume engine, and it's where most solar campaigns quietly fail. The default mistake: instant forms with two fields, optimized for lead volume. You'll get $15 'leads' and your setters will burn out dialing renters, shaded roofs, and 580 credit scores.

The fix is friction engineering. Build your form or landing page to qualify on the four things that actually kill solar deals: homeownership, average monthly electric bill (ask for a range — $150+ is the floor in most markets), credit self-assessment, and roof type. Yes, your cost per lead rises from $15 to $45–$80. Your cost per qualified lead drops, because you stop paying setters to disqualify garbage.

On creative, the winners in solar right now share a pattern: local specificity beats national polish. A talking-head video referencing the actual utility ('If CPS Energy raised your bill again this year…') will outperform a drone shot of panels every time. Run 6–10 creative variants into a consolidated campaign structure — broad targeting, let the qualification friction do the filtering — and kill anything above your CPL ceiling within 3–4 days.

Benchmarks to hold your buyer to: $45–$80 per bill-qualified lead, 60%+ contact rate with sub-5-minute speed to lead, and 25–35% lead-to-appointment. If your Meta program can't hit those, the problem is almost always the offer or the form — not the algorithm.

Channel 2: Google for the demand you didn't create

Meta interrupts homeowners who weren't thinking about solar. Google captures the ones who already are — the homeowner who just opened a brutal summer bill and typed 'solar panel cost' plus your city. That click is expensive ($8–$25 in most metros, higher in saturated ones) and worth every cent, because search intent converts to appointments at 2–3x social rates.

Structure matters more than budget here. Split campaigns into three intent tiers: high-intent commercial terms ('solar installers near me', 'solar quotes [city]'), cost-research terms ('solar panel cost', 'is solar worth it in [state]'), and competitor/brand terms. Bid aggressively on tier one, moderately on tier two with a strong cost-calculator landing page, and surgically on tier three.

Two force multipliers most solar companies skip. First, Google Local Services Ads — pay-per-lead, Google-screened badge, and it sits above regular ads. Second, call extensions with tracking numbers routed straight to setters, because a meaningful share of solar searchers are 55+ and simply prefer to call.

The portfolio logic: Google leads cost more per unit but close 1.5–2x better, while Meta scales volume Google's search inventory can't match. Run Meta at roughly 60–70% of paid budget and Google at 30–40%, and let closed-deal data — tracked in your CRM, not platform dashboards — rebalance the split quarterly. Judge the system on blended cost per install, never on either channel in isolation.

Channel 3: Database reactivation — the free pipeline you're sitting on

Every solar company more than a year old is sitting on a graveyard of unclosed opportunities: old aggregator leads, canceled appointments, homeowners who said 'not right now' in 2024, quotes that died in finance. Most CRMs hold 2,000–10,000 of these contacts. This is the cheapest pipeline you will ever touch, and almost nobody works it systematically.

The mechanism is simple. Load the dormant list into an automation platform — GoHighLevel is the standard play here — and run a 5–7 touch SMS and email sequence over two weeks. The message that works is not 'checking in.' It's a reason-to-reopen: utility rate increases since they last quoted ('Rates in your area went up 11% since we talked'), expiring incentive angles, or a no-pressure re-quote offer since panel pricing shifted.

Expect 5–15% of a dormant database to respond and 1–3% to book. On a 5,000-contact list, that's 50–150 booked conversations for the cost of SMS sends — call it $300–$500 all-in. Layer a conversational AI or a single setter on response handling and the economics get absurd: reactivation deals routinely land at under $200 cost per install versus $2,000–$3,000 from cold paid traffic.

Run reactivation quarterly, not once. A 'no' in March is a 'maybe' in August when the bill doubles. The list regenerates its own value every time the utility raises rates — which, reliably, it does.

Speed to lead: where solar deals actually die

The three channels above generate the raw material. Whether it becomes revenue is decided in the first five minutes after the lead lands — and this is where most solar companies bleed out. MIT's classic lead-response research found contact odds drop roughly 10x when response time slips from five minutes to thirty. In solar, where the homeowner just filled out forms for you and two competitors, the first dial usually owns the deal.

Build the machine so speed isn't dependent on human discipline. Lead hits the CRM, and three things fire instantly: an SMS acknowledging the request with a booking link (Calendly or your CRM's native calendar), an automated dial connecting your setter to the lead within 60 seconds, and an email with social proof — installs in their neighborhood, review screenshots, a 90-second explainer video.

If no answer, the cadence continues: 6–8 touches across SMS, calls, and email over five days, front-loaded into day one. Add an AI voice agent or after-hours answering layer and your effective response window becomes 24/7 — which matters, because a third of solar leads come in evenings and weekends when your setters are off.

The operators hitting 65–80% contact rates aren't hiring superhuman setters. They've just removed every gap where a lead can sit untouched. Audit your own funnel this week: pull timestamps on your last 50 leads and measure lead-arrival to first-dial. If the median is over five minutes, fix that before spending another dollar on ads.

The math: what this stack should cost and return

Here's the full model on a realistic mid-size budget. Say $15,000/month in paid media: $10,000 to Meta, $5,000 to Google, plus roughly $500 in reactivation and automation costs.

Meta at a $65 blended CPL yields ~150 qualified leads. At 30% lead-to-appointment and a 65% sit rate, that's ~29 sat appointments. Google at $110 per lead (blending search CPLs and LSA) yields ~45 leads converting to appointments at 40% — call it 18 sits, and better-qualified ones. Quarterly reactivation, amortized monthly, adds another 10–15 booked conversations at near-zero cost. Total: roughly 55–60 sat appointments a month.

At a 25% close rate — conservative for a competent in-home or virtual close process — that's 13–15 installs. Against ~$15,500 total acquisition spend, you're at $1,050–$1,200 cost per install. On deals grossing $25,000–$35,000 with healthy margin, customer acquisition lands around 4% of contract value. Door-heavy programs routinely run 2–3x that once you fully load rep wages, management, and churn.

Track it in one place. Meta Ads Manager will claim credit for everything, Google Analytics tells a different story, and neither knows what funded. The number that governs decisions is CRM-verified cost per installed deal by source. Review it monthly, rebalance budget quarterly, and ignore any agency that reports success in link clicks.

How to sequence the rollout over 90 days

Don't launch all three channels at once — you'll blur attribution and overwhelm your setters. Sequence it.

Days 1–14: Infrastructure first. CRM pipeline stages defined, tracking numbers provisioned, speed-to-lead automations built and tested, qualification form drafted. Launching ads before this exists is how companies pay for leads that rot in an inbox. This phase costs almost nothing and determines everything.

Days 15–45: Meta live. Launch 6–10 creatives against your qualified-form flow at a starting budget you can hold steady for three weeks — algorithmic learning needs consistency more than size. Expect the first two weeks to run 20–30% above target CPL while the pixel seasons. Kill losing creatives weekly; don't touch campaign structure for at least 14 days.

Days 30–60: Google layers in. Start with LSA and one exact-match high-intent search campaign. By now your setters have reps handling Meta volume, and your CRM data shows true contact and sit rates, so you can calculate what a Google lead is actually worth to you before bidding aggressively.

Days 45–90: Reactivation fires. Clean the dormant list, run the first two-week sequence, and book the wave of re-opened conversations into an already-warm calendar operation.

By day 90 you have three independent lead sources, real cost-per-install data on each, and an acquisition system that doesn't collapse when a canvassing manager takes a competitor's offer.

The bottom line

The best lead generation strategy for solar companies isn't a channel — it's a system: Meta for scalable volume, Google for high-intent capture, database reactivation for near-free pipeline, all wired into a speed-to-lead engine that answers in minutes, not hours. Each piece covers the others' weaknesses, and every dollar builds audience data and CRM assets you own — not an aggregator's.

The operators winning residential solar over the next few years won't be the ones with the biggest door armies. They'll be the ones who treated customer acquisition like infrastructure: measured to the installed deal, rebalanced on real numbers, and compounding quarter after quarter while competitors keep renting shared leads and re-recruiting canvassers.

faq.question: What is a good cost per lead for solar companies?
faq.answer: For exclusive, self-generated leads with qualification friction (homeownership, bill size, credit self-assessment), expect $45–$80 on Meta and $80–$150 on Google search. Cheaper leads exist, but unqualified $15 form fills usually cost more per installed deal once you account for setter time and dead conversations. The metric that matters is cost per install — typically $1,000–$1,500 with a well-run stack.

faq.question: Are purchased solar leads from aggregators worth it?
faq.answer: Rarely. Aggregator leads are typically sold to 3–5 installers simultaneously, contact at 30–40%, and close at 2–5% — which often puts effective lead cost per install at $2,500 or more. Exclusive self-generated leads contact at 60–80% with fast follow-up and close at 2–3x the rate. Aggregators can fill short-term capacity gaps, but they build no owned assets.

faq.question: Should solar companies stop door-knocking entirely?
faq.answer: Not necessarily — the model should change. Field teams close well in the home, so the smart play is using paid media and reactivation to generate pre-qualified appointments, then deploying your best in-person closers against them. What no longer pencils is using hourly canvassers as your primary lead generation layer, where true cost per sat appointment often exceeds $200–$300.

faq.question: How fast should we follow up with a new solar lead?
faq.answer: Under five minutes, every time. Lead-response research shows contact odds fall roughly 10x between minute five and minute thirty, and solar homeowners typically submit to multiple installers at once — the first dial usually owns the deal. Automate an instant SMS, a sub-60-second connect call, and a follow-up email, and cover evenings and weekends with an AI voice agent or answering layer.

faq.question: What is database reactivation and does it work for solar?
faq.answer: Database reactivation is running structured SMS and email sequences to dormant contacts already in your CRM — old leads, canceled appointments, dead quotes. In solar it works unusually well because the pain (a rising electric bill) resurfaces monthly. Expect 5–15% response and 1–3% booked conversations per campaign, at a cost per install frequently under $200. Run it quarterly.

Each channel plays a distinct role. Running only one is why most solar companies get mediocre results and blame "Meta doesn't work anymore." Here's the split we recommend for a solar company spending $30K-$100K/month on paid: - Meta Ads (60-65% of budget): Volume driver. Cold traffic, homeowner targeting, utility-bill-focused creative. This is where you generate the top-of-funnel lead volume.

  • YouTube Ads (15-20% of budget): Trust and mid-funnel. In-stream ads targeting homeowners researching solar, energy costs, tax credits. Warms the pixel and lifts Meta performance.
  • Google LSA + Search (20-25% of budget): Bottom-funnel capture. High-intent "solar installer near me" traffic. Expensive per click but converts at 15-25%. The magic isn't any single channel. It's the interaction. YouTube views cheapen your Meta leads. Meta lead volume feeds retargeting pools. Google LSA catches the ready-to-buy homeowner who saw you on Meta three weeks ago. Attribution in Meta Ads Manager will underreport this. Trust the blended CPL, not the platform-reported one.

Meta Ads: the creative and offer that gets under $80 CPL

Meta is where solar campaigns live or die. Two things matter: the offer and the creative angle. Everything else (audiences, placements, bidding) is now largely automated by Advantage+ campaigns and works fine out of the box. Stop running "free solar quote" offers. Everyone runs that. Instead, lead with a utility bill reduction hook tied to a specific state incentive. Examples that are working: - "Texas homeowners: see how much of your electric bill you can eliminate before the 30% federal credit steps down"

  • "Florida homeowners with a $200+ power bill — check if your roof qualifies for $0-down solar"
  • "Your utility just raised rates again. Here's what solar actually costs in [city] this month." Creative format that's winning: UGC-style video, 30-45 seconds, shot vertically. A real homeowner or installer talking to camera about their power bill going from $340 to $12. No stock footage. No drone shots of panels. Founders who spend $2K getting 8-10 UGC ads made monthly are crushing agencies still running static image ads. Use Meta's Instant Forms with 4 qualifying questions: homeowner status, monthly electric bill ($150+ minimum), roof condition, and timeline. Push leads via webhook straight into GoHighLevel or HubSpot. Speed-to-lead under 5 minutes should be non-negotiable — text and call within 90 seconds if you can automate it.

YouTube and Google LSA: the trust and intent layer

YouTube is the most underused channel in solar. In-stream ads (the ones before videos) run at $0.03-$0.08 per view. You're paying pennies to put a 2-minute educational video in front of homeowners actively researching solar, tax credits, or energy costs. It doesn't generate a ton of direct-response leads, but it does two things that matter: it lifts Meta conversion rates by 20-40% and it builds a retargeting pool of warm viewers. Build one core YouTube asset: a 90-second to 3-minute video that explains how solar actually works financially in your state — federal credit, state incentive, net metering rules, real numbers. Not a pitch. Education. Then run it as an in-stream ad targeting homeowners in your service area with custom intent audiences built from search terms like "solar cost," "solar tax credit 2026," and competitor names. Google Local Services Ads (LSA) is the other must-have. It's pay-per-lead, sits above regular search results, and captures the highest-intent traffic in your market. Expect $60-$120 per LSA lead but close rates of 20-30% because these people are ready. You need Google verification, real reviews (aim for 50+ at 4.7+ stars), and fast response to every ping. Miss a lead call and Google demotes you. Run standard Google Search alongside LSA for keyword coverage LSA doesn't fill — brand terms, long-tail like "solar installer [neighborhood]," and competitor conquest.

Database reactivation: the free channel every solar company ignores

Here's the play that costs almost nothing and pulls 15-40 appointments in the first 14 days for most solar companies: reactivate every unclosed lead from the last 24 months. If you've been in business more than two years, you're sitting on 2,000-20,000 old leads. Most of them said "not right now," "my roof needs work first," "waiting on tax return," or ghosted. Circumstances have changed for a huge chunk of them. Utility rates went up. The federal tax credit timeline shifted. They finally replaced the roof. They're ready — they just haven't heard from you in 8 months. The sequence, built in GoHighLevel or HubSpot: 1. SMS 1 (Day 1): "Hey [name], it's [rep] with [company]. — utility rates in [city] jumped again. Still interested in a quick check on what solar would cost you now? Reply YES or NO." 2. SMS 2 (Day 3, to non-responders): "Quick one — federal credit is still 30% but that steps down. Worth 60 seconds to see updated numbers?" 3. Email (Day 5): Case study of a similar homeowner with specific savings numbers. 4. Voicemail drop (Day 7): Ringless voicemail from the owner or lead rep. 5. Final SMS (Day 12): Break-up message with a soft opt-out. Expected numbers on a 5,000-record list: 8-15% reply rate, 3-5% appointment rate, 150-250 appointments booked. Cost: your SMS spend (about $0.015 per message) and the tech stack. Effective CPL: $5-$15. This should run quarterly, not once.

The tech stack and speed-to-lead that makes this work

None of this stack works without infrastructure. Leads coming in from four sources need to hit one place, get scored, and get contacted in under 5 minutes. Here's the minimum viable stack: - CRM: GoHighLevel (best for solar/home services under $10M) or HubSpot (better if you're scaling past $20M and need real reporting). Salesforce is overkill unless you're running a 100+ rep operation.

  • Lead routing: Zapier or native webhooks from Meta, Google, and website forms into the CRM. Every lead source tagged clearly.
  • Speed-to-lead automation: Instant SMS on lead submission ("Hey [name], [rep] here — got your info about solar. Can I call you now or in 10 min?"), auto-dial trigger to the assigned rep's phone, fallback to team if unanswered in 60 seconds.
  • Appointment booking: Calendly or GoHighLevel's native calendar embedded in follow-up SMS.
  • Reporting: A single dashboard showing CPL by source, appointment set rate, appointment show rate, close rate, and revenue per lead. Update weekly. The biggest leak in most solar operations isn't lead volume — it's speed and follow-up. Leads contacted in 5 minutes vs. 30 minutes close at 21x the rate (MIT study, still holds). If your reps aren't hitting new leads within 5 minutes 90%+ of the time, no ad strategy fixes that.

KPIs and benchmarks to hold your team accountable to

You can't manage what you don't measure, and "we got a lot of leads this month" isn't a KPI. Here's what to track weekly on a solar paid + reactivation program running at $30K-$100K/month: - Cost per lead (blended): Target $60-$90 for qualified leads (homeowner, $150+ bill, decision-maker).

  • Lead-to-appointment set rate: 25-40% is healthy. Under 20% means your qualification is broken or speed-to-lead is slow.
  • Appointment show rate: 55-70%. Under 50%, your confirmation sequence is weak.
  • Show-to-close rate: 20-35% on Meta leads, 25-40% on LSA, 15-25% on reactivation.
  • Cost per acquisition (installed customer): $600-$1,200 in most markets. Above $1,500 and the model needs work.
  • Speed-to-first-contact: Median under 5 minutes, 90th percentile under 15 minutes. Review these on a weekly ops call, not monthly. Kill campaigns where CPL is 40%+ above target for 7 days. Double budget on campaigns hitting target with volume headroom. Most solar companies are afraid to scale spend fast enough — if a campaign is producing $70 leads that close, pour on the gas until it breaks. Then diagnose and rebuild.

The bottom line

The best lead generation strategy for solar companies isn't a single tactic — it's a stack. Meta for volume, YouTube for trust, Google LSA for intent, and database reactivation for the free money you're already sitting on. Built correctly with fast follow-up and clean attribution, this consistently produces qualified leads under $80 and installed customers under $1,200 in most U.S. markets. The operators winning in solar right now aren't the ones with the biggest canvassing teams. They're the ones who built a paid acquisition machine, own their database, and treat speed-to-lead like a religion. If you're still running the 2019 playbook, you're not just leaving money on the table — you're funding your competitors' scale.

faq.question: How much should a solar company spend on ads per month to see results?
faq.answer: Minimum $15K/month to get statistically meaningful data across Meta, YouTube, and Google LSA. Under that, you're guessing. Companies serious about scaling typically run $30K-$100K/month and see CPLs drop as the pixel matures and creative library expands.

faq.question: How long until a paid solar lead gen program hits sub-$80 CPL?
faq.answer: Expect 30-60 days of learning. Weeks 1-3 you'll see $120-$180 CPLs as Meta's algorithm learns. By week 6-8 with 8-12 creative variations tested and audiences optimized, sub-$80 is realistic in most markets. Slower in ultra-competitive metros like Los Angeles or Phoenix.

faq.question: Is door-knocking completely dead for solar?
faq.answer: No, but it should be a supplement, not the core strategy. Door-knocking still works for finishing deals on homes near an active install or in targeted HOAs. As a primary lead source, the unit economics no longer pencil out for most markets.

faq.question: Should I use a solar-specific lead vendor or run my own ads?
faq.answer: Run your own ads. Shared lead vendors sell the same lead 3-5 times and your close rate collapses. Exclusive lead vendors charge $200-$400 per lead with no control over volume or quality. Owned paid channels give you control, better economics at scale, and a compounding database asset.

faq.question: What's a realistic close rate on Meta solar leads?
faq.answer: 8-15% lead-to-installed-customer for well-run operations. Broken down: 30% lead-to-appointment-set, 60% appointment-show, 25% show-to-close. If you're under 5% overall, the problem is almost always speed-to-lead, qualification questions, or sales process — not the ads.

articles.title: Google Local Services Ads vs Google Ads for Contractors
articles.description: LSAs or Google Search for contractor leads? A cost-per-booked-job breakdown showing when each wins — and when stacking both prints money.
articles.keyword: facebook ads budget for med spa
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most contractors are asking the wrong question. It's not "which platform is cheaper per lead" — it's which platform delivers the cheapest booked job, because a $28 LSA lead that never answers the phone is more expensive than a $95 Search lead that closes at 40%.

We've managed both channels for home-service clients across HVAC, plumbing, roofing, and electrical, and the pattern is consistent: contractors who treat LSAs and Google Ads as an either/or decision leave 30–50% of their bookable demand on the table. The ones who stack both — with the right budget split — own the entire results page for their highest-intent searches.

Here's the side-by-side breakdown: real cost mechanics, where each channel wins, and the exact scenarios where running both stacked is the only correct answer.

How the two channels actually charge you

Local Services Ads are pay-per-lead. You're charged when a homeowner calls or messages through the LSA unit — typically $25–$95 per lead depending on trade and market. Roofing and water damage sit at the top of that range; garage door and locksmith at the bottom. You can dispute junk leads (wrong service area, spam, solicitors) and Google credits a meaningful percentage back when you actually file disputes. Most contractors never do, which quietly inflates their real cost per lead by 15–20%.

Google Ads (Search) is pay-per-click. You pay $8–$50+ per click for terms like "emergency plumber near me" whether or not anyone contacts you. Your cost per lead is a function of click price times landing page conversion rate. A $20 click with a 15% converting page is a $133 lead. Same click with a 30% converting page is a $67 lead — which is why Search performance is really a landing page problem wearing a media-buying costume.

The structural difference matters: LSAs shift conversion risk onto Google. Search puts it on you. That's why LSAs feel safer — and why they cap out, because Google controls your volume, your ranking, and increasingly your price per lead. With Search, you control the throttle.

The cost-per-booked-job math, side by side

Take a mid-market HVAC company as the model. LSA leads at $55 each. Answer rate on LSA calls is high — the homeowner initiated a phone call, so 70–80% connect. Booking rate on connected calls runs 50–60% for a decent CSR. Net: roughly $110–$130 per booked job.

Now Search: $22 average CPC, landing page converting at 18%, so $122 per lead. But lead mix is different — 60% calls, 40% forms, and form leads book at half the rate of calls. Blended booking rate lands around 35–45%. Net: $270–$350 per booked job.

On that math LSAs win by 2–3x, and for straightforward repair demand, they usually do. But run the same math on a $12,000 system replacement instead of a $400 repair call: Search lets you target "HVAC replacement cost" and "new AC unit financing" — buyers LSAs can't isolate, because LSA gives you almost no query-level control. A $300 booked job cost against a $12K ticket with 40% gross margin is a rounding error.

The verdict isn't "LSAs are cheaper." It's: LSAs are cheaper for demand you can't differentiate. Search is cheaper for demand you can select. Track cost per booked job by job type — in GoHighLevel or even a spreadsheet — and this becomes obvious in your own numbers within 60 days.

Where LSAs beat Search outright

Three scenarios where LSAs should get the first dollar every time.

Emergency and repair demand. "AC not cooling," "burst pipe," "garage door stuck" — the homeowner wants the first credible company that answers. The LSA unit sits above every paid ad and organic result, shows the Google Guaranteed badge, and drives a direct phone call. Speed-to-answer wins these jobs, and LSAs are built for exactly that motion.

Trust-gated trades. Locksmiths, appliance repair, house cleaning — categories where homeowners are actively worried about scams. The Google Guaranteed badge (backed by Google's up-to-$2,000 reimbursement) does real conversion work that no landing page can replicate.

Thin marketing infrastructure. If a contractor has no converting landing page, no call tracking, and no one managing negative keywords, Search will bleed them dry. LSAs are the correct crawl-before-you-walk channel: no landing page required, no keyword management, and disputes as a safety net.

One more advantage nobody prices in: LSA rank is heavily driven by review count, review velocity, and answer rate — assets you build anyway. A contractor with 400 reviews and a 90% answer rate gets outsized LSA volume at the same per-lead price as a competitor with 40 reviews. Search gives you no such compounding loyalty; you re-buy every click at auction.

Where Google Ads wins and LSAs can't compete

High-ticket, research-phase buyers. LSAs fire on service-provider searches, but they can't isolate "HVAC replacement financing," "metal roof vs shingles cost," or "whole home repipe." Those queries are your $10K–$40K tickets, and Search is the only paid channel on Google that lets you bid on them directly with a page built to convert that specific job.

Volume control and scale. LSA volume is capped by your market, your rank, and Google's pacing — many contractors max out their LSA budget and simply can't force more leads out of it. Search scales with budget. When you need to fill a second crew's schedule next month, you raise budgets and expand keywords tonight. No LSA lever does that.

Query-level intelligence. Search terms reports tell you exactly what people typed before they called. That feeds your negative keyword list, your service page strategy, and even which services to advertise next. LSAs are a black box — you get a lead category and little else.

Remarketing and the full stack. Search click traffic builds audiences you can remarket to across YouTube and Display for pennies. In Google Analytics you can watch a homeowner click a Tuesday search ad and convert off a Friday remarketing touch. LSA traffic never touches your site, so it builds nothing. Every LSA dollar is a dead end the moment the call ends; every Search dollar leaves a data asset behind.

The stacked play: owning the whole results page

For most established contractors, the right answer is both — because of how the search results page is physically laid out. On a high-intent local query, the page runs: LSA carousel, then paid Search ads, then the map pack, then organic. A contractor running LSAs plus Search plus a strong Google Business Profile can hold three of the top four screen positions. Your competitor running only one channel appears once, below you.

That's not redundancy — it's suppression. Every slot you occupy is a slot a competitor doesn't. Click studies consistently show the majority of clicks and calls never scroll past the first screen on mobile, and mobile is 70%+ of emergency home-service search.

The budget split we run for stacked accounts: LSAs funded to their natural cap first (they'll rarely spend more than the market gives them), then Search takes the remainder, weighted toward high-ticket and replacement keywords LSAs can't reach. For a $6K/month contractor budget, that typically lands around $2K LSA / $4K Search. For a $2K budget, it's usually $1,500 LSA / $500 brand-and-emergency Search — or LSA-only until the budget grows.

Measure the stack as one system. If LSA cost per booked job is $120 and Search is $300 but Search jobs average 4x the ticket, the stack is healthy. Judge each channel against the jobs it's actually assigned to win.

The operational layer that decides who profits

Both channels are won or lost after the lead arrives, and this is where most contractor ad budgets actually die.

Answer rate is the whole game on LSAs. Google tracks it and ranks you accordingly; miss calls and your volume drops while your competitors' rises. If nobody can answer within three rings during business hours, fix that before spending another dollar — with a trained CSR, an answering service, or an AI voice agent that answers 24/7 and books directly into the calendar. Missed-call text-back through GoHighLevel recovers a portion of what still slips through.

Dispute LSA leads weekly. Wrong service area, spam, solicitation, duplicate — file them. Contractors who dispute rigorously recover 10–20% of spend. That's a margin line item, not an admin chore.

Track to booked job, not lead. CallRail or GoHighLevel call tracking on Search, plus job outcomes logged against source. Within 90 days you'll know your true cost per booked job by channel and by job type — and budget decisions become arithmetic instead of arguments.

Feed conversions back to Google. Import booked-job conversions (offline conversion tracking) so Smart Bidding optimizes toward jobs, not form fills. Accounts that do this routinely cut cost per booked job 20–30% inside two quarters, because Google stops optimizing for the wrong event.

A 90-day rollout plan that de-risks the decision

Days 1–14: LSA foundation. Get Google Guaranteed verification moving immediately — background checks and license verification take one to three weeks, so start now. Meanwhile, push your review engine: every completed job gets a review request same-day. Set up call tracking and a call-answering standard (three rings, live human or AI agent, book on the first call).

Days 15–45: LSA live, baseline established. Run LSAs at a budget the market can absorb. Dispute junk weekly. Log every lead to outcome. By day 45 you have a real cost-per-booked-job number, not a guess.

Days 45–75: layer Search where LSAs can't reach. Launch tightly-themed campaigns for your high-ticket services — replacements, installs, remodels — each with a dedicated landing page. Exact and phrase match only to start; broad match with no data is a donation to Google. Brand campaign at $5–10/day to protect your name from competitors bidding on it (they are).

Days 75–90: judge with data. Compare cost per booked job by channel and job type. Kill what's above your allowable acquisition cost, feed what's below it. Most contractors who run this sequence keep both channels — LSAs harvesting emergency demand, Search hunting big tickets — because the math tells them to, not because an agency did.

The bottom line

LSAs versus Google Ads was never a fair fight — they're different weapons for different demand. LSAs win the race to emergency and repair calls at the lowest cost per booked job in the account. Search wins the high-ticket, research-phase buyer LSAs can't even see, and it's the only lever that scales on command.

The contractors compounding fastest run both, measure to booked job instead of lead, and treat answer rate and offline conversion tracking as seriously as the media buying itself. Own the whole first screen for your best searches and the channel debate resolves itself — in your P&L, not in a blog comment section.

faq.question: Are Google Local Services Ads worth it for contractors?
faq.answer: For emergency and repair-driven trades — HVAC, plumbing, electrical, garage door — yes, almost always. LSA cost per booked job typically runs $100–$180, well below what most contractors achieve on Search for the same demand. The caveats: volume is capped by your market and rank, you must answer calls fast (Google ranks you on it), and you should dispute junk leads weekly to recover 10–20% of spend.

faq.question: Why are my LSA leads so expensive lately?
faq.answer: Three usual causes: more competitors verified in your category (auction pressure raises per-lead pricing), a declining answer rate or review velocity pushing your rank down so you only win pricier lead types, and undisputed junk leads inflating your real average. Audit answer rate first, restart your review engine second, and file disputes on every wrong-area, spam, and solicitation lead — most contractors reclaim 10–20% of spend.

faq.question: Should a contractor run LSAs and Google Ads at the same time?
faq.answer: If the budget supports both, yes — they occupy different positions on the results page, so running both means holding two to three of the top screen slots on your highest-intent searches. Fund LSAs to their natural cap first (emergency/repair demand), then put remaining budget into Search targeting high-ticket keywords LSAs can't reach, like replacements and installs. Judge each channel by cost per booked job for the job types it's assigned.

faq.question: How much do Local Services Ads cost per lead?
faq.answer: Typically $25–$95 per lead depending on trade and metro. Locksmith and garage door sit at the low end; roofing, water damage restoration, and HVAC replacement markets at the high end. Remember you pay per lead, not per booked job — so a $55 lead with a 55% booking rate is really a ~$100 booked job. Track that second number; it's the one that decides your budget.

faq.question: What's a good cost per booked job from Google Ads for home services?
faq.answer: It depends entirely on ticket size. For repair work ($300–$800 tickets), $150–$250 per booked job is workable and under $150 is strong. For replacements and installs ($8K–$40K tickets), $300–$600 per booked job is comfortably profitable at typical margins. Set your allowable per job type — roughly 10–15% of average ticket for repair, 3–5% for big-ticket — and manage campaigns against those lines, not against a blended average.

articles.title: Google Local Services Ads vs Google Ads for Contractors: CPBJ Breakdown
articles.description: LSAs vs Google Search Ads for contractors: real cost-per-booked-job math, when each wins, and the stacked setup that prints jobs.
articles.keyword: google local services ads vs google ads for contractors
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most contractors running paid media are lighting money on fire in one of two ways: they're all-in on Google Ads with a $180 cost-per-lead and a 22% booking rate, or they're relying solely on Local Services Ads (LSAs) and capping growth the moment Google throttles their impressions. Both are wrong. The right answer depends on your service, your ticket size, and your close rate — and once you know the math, running both stacked is almost always the winner. This is for HVAC, roofing, plumbing, electrical, remodeling, and home services operators doing $500K–$20M who want to stop guessing which channel deserves the next $10K. We're going to break down cost-per-booked-job (CPBJ) on both channels using real ranges, show you the exact scenarios where LSAs crush Search and vice versa, and give you a stacking playbook that pushes blended CPBJ down 30–50%. By the end, you'll know which channel to fund first, what to expect per dollar, and how to structure both accounts so they feed each other instead of bidding against themselves.

The only metric that matters: cost-per-booked-job

Forget CPC. Forget CPL. If you're a contractor, the metric that pays your payroll is cost-per-booked-job (CPBJ) — total ad spend divided by jobs that actually got on the schedule and paid. Here's why lead-level metrics lie: LSAs and Google Search Ads have wildly different lead qualities. An LSA lead is a phone call from someone who tapped your Google profile after seeing reviews and a green checkmark. A Search Ad lead is often a form fill from someone comparing five contractors. Book rates diverge by 2-3x. Quick math to run on your own data: - Google Ads CPBJ: Spend ÷ (Leads × Book Rate). Example: $6,000 spend, 40 leads, 25% book rate = 10 jobs = $600 CPBJ.

  • LSAs CPBJ: Spend ÷ Booked Jobs (dispute unqualified leads to lower spend). Example: $6,000 spend, 35 valid leads, 55% book rate = 19 jobs = $316 CPBJ. Before you compare channels, tag every lead source in your CRM (ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, Jobber, or GoHighLevel) and calculate CPBJ monthly. If you can't do this, you're not ready to scale either channel — fix tracking first.

How Google Local Services Ads actually work

LSAs sit at the very top of the search results, above traditional Google Ads. You pay per lead (call or message), not per click. To run them, you must pass Google's screening: license verification, insurance, and background checks for owners and field techs. That gate is why LSAs convert — searchers trust the Google Guaranteed badge. Key mechanics contractors miss: - Lead price varies by trade and market: HVAC leads run $25–$75, roofing $35–$120, plumbing $20–$60, remodeling $50–$200. Your bid strategy (max per lead vs max spend) affects volume more than most realize.

  • Reviews drive ranking harder than bid: An account with 80+ 5-star Google reviews at 4.9 stars will out-rank a higher bidder with 20 reviews. Job one is a review engine (NiceJob, Podium, or a GoHighLevel automation firing 30 min post-close).
  • You can dispute bad leads: Wrong service area, spam, wrong service — Google refunds them, often 8–15% of leads. Contractors who don't dispute are overpaying by that same margin.
  • Response time matters: Google measures pickup rate. Miss calls, your ranking tanks. Route to a live answering service (Nexa, Ruby) if you can't hit 90%+. LSAs are pay-per-lead, but the lead is warmer, the intent is higher, and the trust signal is already built in before your phone rings.

How Google Search Ads work for contractors (and where they leak money)

Traditional Google Search Ads (the sponsored results below LSAs) are pay-per-click. You bid on keywords, write ad copy, drive to a landing page, and hope the form fills or call comes in. On paper, more control. In practice, more leaks. Where contractors bleed money on Search: 1. Broad match with no negatives: Bidding on "AC repair" without excluding "DIY," "parts," "how to," "jobs" burns 20–40% of spend on non-buyers. 2. Sending traffic to the homepage: Homepages convert at 2–4%. A dedicated service-page landing (built in Unbounce, Instapage, or a GoHighLevel funnel) with call button above the fold, reviews, and a single offer converts at 8–15%. 3. No call tracking: If you're not using CallRail or CallTrackingMetrics with dynamic number insertion, you can't tell which keyword produced the booked job. You're optimizing blind. 4. Ignoring device split: 70%+ of contractor searches are mobile. Desktop-heavy landing pages tank conversion. Benchmarks I see across HVAC, roofing, and plumbing accounts: CPC $8–$28, conversion rate 8–14% on a proper landing page, book rate 20–35% from Search leads (lower than LSAs because the searcher hasn't seen your reviews yet). Blended, that's a CPBJ of $450–$900 for a well-run account, $1,200+ for a sloppy one.

Side-by-side CPBJ breakdown: LSAs vs Google Ads

Here's what the math actually looks like for a mid-sized HVAC contractor spending $10K/month on each channel in a Tier 2 metro: Local Services Ads

  • Spend: $10,000
  • Leads at $45 avg: 222
  • Disputed/refunded (12%): -27 leads
  • Valid leads: 195
  • Book rate: 50%
  • Booked jobs: 97
  • CPBJ: $103 Google Search Ads
  • Spend: $10,000
  • Clicks at $14 avg CPC: 714
  • Conversion rate (calls + forms): 11%
  • Leads: 78
  • Book rate: 28%
  • Booked jobs: 22
  • CPBJ: $455 At first glance, LSAs demolish Search — 4.4x more efficient. But this is where operators make the wrong call. LSAs will cap out in your market. Google only shows 3 LSA slots and rotates a limited pool. Once you've captured your available share (usually $8K–$25K/month depending on metro and trade), incremental spend does nothing. Search Ads, by contrast, scale further. And Search wins on specific job types: high-ticket remodels, commercial work, and niche services where the searcher wants to read a page before calling. LSAs dominate emergency and same-day trades (burst pipe, no heat, roof leak). Search wins on considered purchases (kitchen remodel, roof replacement, panel upgrade). The rule of thumb: LSAs first, Search second, always both eventually.

When LSAs win outright

Fund LSAs before touching Search if you match any of these: - Emergency/same-day service dominant: Plumbing leaks, HVAC no-cool/no-heat, garage door won't open, locksmith. Intent is 10/10 and searchers call the first credible option. LSAs are that option.

  • Average ticket under $2,000: Service calls, tune-ups, small repairs. Search CPBJ eats the margin. LSAs at $80–$150 CPBJ leave room.
  • Strong review profile: 50+ Google reviews at 4.7+. You'll dominate the LSA carousel and pull leads below the market average cost.
  • Small team, limited landing page infrastructure: LSAs don't need a website funnel. Your Google Business Profile IS the landing page.
  • New to paid media: LSAs are lower-skill to run well. You dispute bad leads, keep response time high, ask for reviews. Search Ads punish beginners. I've onboarded roofing and plumbing clients where we pushed LSA spend to $18K/month before touching Google Ads and hit CPBJ under $150. If your market has room and your reviews are strong, exhaust LSAs first. It's the cheapest booked job you'll ever buy.

When Google Search Ads win outright

There are real scenarios where Search beats LSAs on booked-job economics: - High-ticket, considered purchases: Full roof replacements ($15K–$40K), kitchen remodels ($40K–$150K), whole-home HVAC installs ($10K–$25K). Searchers compare, read, and want detail. A well-built landing page with financing, before/after gallery, and free estimate form converts better than a phone call from LSAs.

  • Commercial work: LSAs are largely residential. B2B searches for "commercial HVAC contractor" or "industrial roofing" belong on Search.
  • Niche services LSAs don't categorize well: Foundation repair, EV charger installation, spray foam insulation, custom pool builds. LSAs force you into broad buckets that misroute leads.
  • Geographic edge markets: If your service area has weak LSA competition data or you serve a wide radius, Search gives you targeting control LSAs can't match.
  • You have a real content and landing page operation: If you have a marketing team running CRO, using Hotjar, iterating headlines monthly — Search rewards that skill. If your average job is $10K+ and you sell on consultation rather than dispatch, Search Ads plus a proper funnel (landing page → phone call or booked estimate via Calendly) will outperform LSAs on revenue per ad dollar even at higher CPBJ.

The stacked playbook: running LSAs and Google Ads together

This is where most contractors leave 30–50% CPBJ reduction on the table. Running both channels correctly stacked creates compounding effects. Here's the setup: 1. Max out LSAs first. Bid to max leads, dispute aggressively, drive review velocity. Establish your CPBJ floor. 2. Add Search Ads targeting only what LSAs can't cover: high-ticket keywords ("roof replacement quote," "new HVAC system cost"), commercial terms, and specific service lines LSAs miscategorize. 3. Use Search Ads for brand defense: Bid on your own brand name. Cheap clicks, blocks competitors, and captures searchers who saw you in LSAs and Googled you to verify. 4. Layer remarketing on Search Ads: Anyone who visited your site but didn't call gets served display and YouTube ads for 30 days. Cheap way to close the loop on LSA callers who didn't book. 5. Feed the CRM back into both: Push offline conversions from ServiceTitan or GoHighLevel back into Google Ads so Smart Bidding optimizes for booked jobs, not form fills. 6. Split budget by CPBJ, not gut: If LSA CPBJ is $120 and Search CPBJ is $480, don't split 50/50. Fund LSAs to saturation, then Search. A stacked account I manage in the roofing space runs 60% LSA / 40% Search and delivers a blended CPBJ of $210 on $40K/month spend. Neither channel could hit that alone.

How to decide this week: a simple decision tree

Stop debating in theory. Run this checklist against your business: Start with LSAs only if:

  • You have 25+ Google reviews at 4.5 stars or better
  • Your average ticket is under $5,000
  • You can answer 90%+ of calls in business hours
  • Your service is dispatch/emergency-oriented Start with Google Search Ads only if:
  • Your average ticket is $10K+ and sells on consultation
  • You have a dedicated landing page (not your homepage)
  • You have call tracking installed (CallRail minimum)
  • You have someone competent running the account (in-house or agency) Run both stacked once:
  • LSA spend has plateaued (adding budget doesn't add leads)
  • You're booking 15+ jobs/month from LSAs
  • You have a CRM tracking source-to-revenue
  • Your close/booking process is documented and consistent If you can't check the boxes for either channel, the answer isn't more ad spend — it's fixing tracking, reviews, and response speed first. Ads amplify what already exists. If the underlying operation leaks, ads leak faster.

The bottom line

LSAs and Google Search Ads aren't competing products — they're different tools for different jobs. LSAs win on efficiency and simplicity, especially for emergency, low-to-mid ticket residential work with a strong review base. Search wins on scale, control, and high-ticket considered purchases. Run LSAs first if you qualify, layer Search on top once LSAs plateau, and measure everything at the cost-per-booked-job level — not the click or lead level. The contractors printing money on Google in 2026 aren't picking a side. They're stacking both channels, feeding CRM data back into the algorithms, and killing waste weekly. Pull your last 90 days of ad spend, calculate CPBJ by channel, and if you can't — that's the first fix before another dollar goes into either account.

faq.question: Can I run LSAs and Google Ads at the same time without them bidding against each other?
faq.answer: Yes. LSAs and Google Search Ads occupy separate ad slots and don't compete in the same auction. Running both actually increases your share of the SERP — you can occupy the LSA carousel AND a top Search Ad position simultaneously, which lifts total click share.

faq.question: How much should a contractor spend on LSAs to know if they work?
faq.answer: Give it 30 days at a minimum of $2,000–$3,000 in spend, assuming you're actively disputing bad leads and requesting reviews. Anything shorter or cheaper doesn't give Google's algorithm enough signal to rank you consistently.

faq.question: Why is my LSA cost-per-lead so much higher than the estimates I see online?
faq.answer: Three usual culprits: weak review profile (under 30 reviews or below 4.5 stars), slow call response tanking your ranking, and not disputing invalid leads. Fix those three and your effective cost-per-lead usually drops 20–40% within 60 days.

faq.question: Should I hire an agency for LSAs or run them in-house?
faq.answer: LSAs are simple enough to run in-house if you have someone dedicated to disputing leads weekly, monitoring response times, and driving review velocity. Google Search Ads are where an experienced agency earns their fee — the technical bar is much higher.

faq.question: Do LSAs work for commercial contractors?
faq.answer: Generally no. LSAs are built around residential service categories and consumer searchers. Commercial contractors get better results from Google Search Ads targeting B2B keywords, paired with LinkedIn Ads for larger accounts.

articles.title: How to Get Clients for a Marketing Agency Without Buying Leads
articles.description: The outbound, authority, and referral system agencies use to fill their pipeline with qualified clients — no lead vendors, no race-to-the-bottom pricing.
articles.keyword: youtube ads for home services lead generation
articles.author: Social Elite Editorial
articles.contentHtml:
Most agencies don't have a client acquisition problem. They have a dependency problem. They rely on referrals that show up whenever they feel like it, a lead vendor selling the same tired list to six competitors, or a founder's personal network that dried up eight months ago. Then they wonder why revenue looks like a heart-rate monitor.

Here's the uncomfortable math: agencies that buy leads from marketplaces like Bark or Thumbtack routinely pay $40–$150 per lead to compete against five other agencies for a prospect who filled out a form on a whim. Close rates on shared leads sit in the 2–8% range. Meanwhile, agencies running a structured outbound-plus-authority system close 20–30% of booked calls — because the prospect came to the conversation already sold on the agency's credibility.

This article lays out the full system: outbound that actually gets replies, authority assets that pre-sell you before the call, and a referral engine that runs on process instead of luck. It's the same pipeline architecture we run internally and build for clients. None of it requires buying a single lead.

Stop competing in lead marketplaces you can't win

Shared-lead platforms are structurally rigged against agencies. The economics only work for the platform: they sell one prospect to multiple buyers, so your differentiation is reduced to who responds fastest and quotes cheapest. You're not selling expertise — you're selling speed and discounts.

Worse, the buyer psychology is wrong. Someone browsing a lead marketplace is comparison shopping on price. Someone who found you through a case study, a referral, or a sharp cold email is evaluating whether you can solve their specific problem. Those are two different sales conversations, and only one of them ends in a retainer at your rates.

Run the numbers on your own data. If you're paying $75 per shared lead, closing 5%, that's a $1,500 customer acquisition cost — for a client anchored on the lowest bid, who churns the moment a cheaper option appears. Compare that to outbound: a well-run cold email system costs roughly $500–$1,000 a month in tooling and data (an Instantly or Smartlead account, verified contact data, a few sending domains) and can book 8–15 qualified calls monthly once dialed in. Same budget, but the clients you close came in on your positioning, not the platform's.

The first move in getting clients for a marketing agency is refusing to acquire them in a commoditized channel. Everything below is how you replace that volume.

Pick a niche your case studies can actually defend

Generalist agencies lose deals to specialists every week, and it's not close. When a personal injury firm compares "we do digital marketing for businesses" against "we generate signed cases for PI firms and here are the cost-per-case numbers from three firms like yours," the specialist wins even at double the price.

Niching isn't about limiting what you can do. It's about what you lead with. Your outbound reply rates, your close rates, and your pricing power all trace back to one question: can the prospect see themselves in your proof?

How to choose without guessing: pull your last ten client engagements and rank them by margin, retention, and results you can quantify. The overlap between "we made them the most money" and "we enjoyed the work" is your niche candidate. Then validate demand — are there at least 5,000 businesses in that vertical that fit your ideal profile? Tools like Apollo or ZoomInfo will tell you in ten minutes.

One warning from experience: pick a vertical where the economics support retainers. A client whose average customer is worth $8,000 (law firms, med spas, home services, lenders) can justify $3,000–$10,000 a month in fees. A client whose average sale is $40 cannot. Your niche determines your ceiling before you send a single email.

Build an outbound engine that books calls every week

Outbound is the only client acquisition channel you fully control. Referrals depend on other people. Inbound takes months to compound. Cold outreach produces conversations this week — if you build it like a system instead of a spam cannon.

The stack: 3–5 secondary sending domains (never your main domain), 2–3 inboxes per domain, warmed for two to three weeks before sending. Instantly, Smartlead, or Apollo handle sending and rotation. Data comes from Apollo or Clay, verified through a tool like MillionVerifier — bad data is the number one silent killer of deliverability.

The message: three sentences, not three paragraphs. Name a specific, observable problem in their business ("you're running Meta ads to a homepage instead of a landing page"), state the outcome you've produced for someone like them with a real number, and ask a low-friction question. No "I hope this finds you well." No feature lists. The entire email should read like a sharp colleague noticed something, not a vendor pitching.

Benchmarks to hold yourself to: 50–70% open rates (a domain health signal), 3–8% reply rates, and roughly one booked call per 150–250 contacts in a decent niche. Volume matters, but only after the message converts — sending 10,000 bad emails just burns domains faster. Start at 30–50 sends per day per inbox, review replies weekly, and iterate the offer, not just the subject line.

Create authority assets that close deals before the call

Cold outreach gets attention. Authority converts it. The gap between a 10% close rate and a 30% close rate is usually what the prospect found when they Googled you between the reply and the call.

The minimum viable authority stack is three assets. First, one flagship case study per niche — not a testimonial, a breakdown: the situation, what you changed, the numbers before and after, with real figures. "We took a roofing company from $180 to $62 per qualified lead in 60 days" does more selling than your entire services page. Second, a founder LinkedIn presence posting two to three times a week about the specific problems your niche faces. Not motivational content — teardown content: what you're seeing in ad accounts, what's working right now, what mistakes you keep finding. Third, a clean website with proof above the fold and a Calendly link, so the path from interest to booked call is one click.

This is also where prospects sniff-test the obvious question: is your own marketing any good? An agency selling SEO with no rankings, or paid ads with a broken pixel on its own site, fails the audit before the first call. Your own presence is a portfolio piece whether you treat it that way or not.

Authority compounds. The same case study that lifts cold email replies also warms referrals, anchors your pricing, and eventually generates inbound. Build these assets once, then let every channel borrow their credibility.

Turn referrals from luck into a process

Referrals are every agency's highest-converting channel — referred prospects close at 3–5x the rate of cold ones and negotiate less. The mistake is treating them as weather instead of infrastructure.

A referral process has three parts. First, timing: ask at the moment of demonstrated value, not at contract renewal. When you send a monthly report showing a win — cost per lead down 40%, best revenue month in a year — that email should end with a specific ask: "Who else in your network is spending on ads without results like these? An intro is the best thank-you we can get." Specific beats generic; "anyone you know" gets ignored, "another franchise owner in your group" gets a name.

Second, incentives: make referring rational. A flat spotter's fee ($500–$1,000 per closed client), a discount on their retainer, or a revenue share for repeat referrers. Put it in writing and mention it at onboarding, so clients know the program exists before you ever ask.

Third, strategic partnerships — the referral channel most agencies never build. Web designers, bookkeepers, business brokers, SaaS account reps, and complementary agencies (you run paid, they do SEO) all talk to your ideal client weekly. Five active partners sending one intro a month outperforms most paid channels, at essentially zero acquisition cost. Track every referral source in your CRM — GoHighLevel or HubSpot both handle this — and review it quarterly like any other channel, because it is one.

Run your own pipeline like a client account

The most credible thing a marketing agency can show a prospect is its own funnel. If you sell paid acquisition, run paid acquisition — even $1,500–$3,000 a month on Meta or Google retargeting the traffic your outbound and content generate. A prospect who got your cold email, saw your case study ad three days later, and then found your LinkedIn post is experiencing your multi-touch competence firsthand.

Treat your pipeline with the same reporting discipline you'd give a client. That means a real CRM with stages (lead → conversation → call booked → proposal → closed), weekly metrics review, and honest attribution. Most agency founders can quote their clients' cost per lead to the dollar and have no idea what their own customer acquisition cost is. That's not a data problem; it's a priority problem.

The numbers that matter: cost per booked call by channel, show rate (below 70% means your booking flow needs friction — qualification questions, confirmation sequences), proposal-to-close rate, and revenue per client per year. When you know these, decisions get simple. If outbound books calls at $180 each and referral partnerships book them at effectively $50, you know where the next hour of effort goes.

Give it 90 days of consistent execution before judging results. Outbound needs two to three sending cycles to dial in, authority content needs a month to accumulate, and referral asks need a reporting cycle to land. Agencies fail at client acquisition mostly by quitting channels at week three.

The 90-day pipeline build, week by week

Here's the sequence, condensed into an executable plan.

Weeks 1–2: Foundation. Pick your niche using the margin-retention-results filter. Write your flagship case study with real numbers. Buy 3–5 sending domains and start warming inboxes. Set up your CRM pipeline stages and a Calendly with two or three qualification questions.
